// How To Use This Workbook

This document is a working tool, not a manual. It has three kinds of page and four kinds of interactive block. Learn the shapes now and the next hundred pages will read themselves.

The three page types
TEACH
WHITE BAND · THE CONCEPT
  • Explains one idea, with real code from the repo
  • Every claim points at a file you can open
  • Ends with a self-check question
LAB
SLATE BAND · HANDS ON KEYBOARD
  • You run commands and change files
  • Expected output is printed so you can compare
  • Deliberate breakage, then repair
GATE
GREEN BAND · PROVE IT
  • Checklist you must pass before moving on
  • Mirrors the real CI gates the repo enforces
  • Signed off by your onboarding lead
The four interactive blocks
  • Checklists — every square box is clickable. Tick it and it stays ticked, even after you close the browser.
  • Answer boxes — the dashed boxes are real text fields. Type in them. Your writing is saved locally.
  • Self-checks — pick an option and it marks itself instantly, then explains why. Wrong answers teach more than right ones, so guess honestly.
  • Progress bar — the teal line along the bottom of the window tracks every box, tick and question in the whole workbook.
Your work is saved in this browser only. It lives in localStorage under one key. Use the same browser and profile throughout the month. Reset in the top bar wipes it deliberately; nothing else will.
How you finish it
Read every pageThe workbook notices which pages you have actually scrolled through. All of them must be seen before the final examination unlocks.
Tick every lab itemEach square box in a LAB or GATE page is a task. The final examination stays locked until every one is ticked.
Sit the examinationTwenty questions drawn at random from all thirteen chapters. 80% to pass, re-sit as often as you like, best score stands.
Collect the certificatePassing unlocks a PDF certificate in your name, carrying your score and a reference number.
Read this in order and do not skip the labs. The chapters build one system across four weeks. Chapter 9 assumes you built the module in Chapter 5. Skipping the keyboard work and reading only the prose is the single most reliable way to finish this document without gaining the ability it promises.

// Before You Start

Five minutes of setup, once. This page is about the workbook itself — where to keep the file, which browser to open it in, and how your progress survives being closed. Do this before Chapter 1, because a workbook that forgets your work is worse than paper.

Step 1 — Put the file somewhere permanent
  • Save PRAXIS_ENGINEERING_WORKBOOK.html to a real folder you own — Documents/JBS Praxis/ is ideal. Not the Downloads folder, and not the Desktop.
  • This matters more than it sounds. Your progress is keyed to the file's location. Move the file later and the browser treats it as a different document, and your ticks and answers will not follow it.
  • Do not rename it. Do not keep two copies open in two tabs — the second one to save wins, and you will lose work.
  • It is a single self-contained file. There is no folder of assets beside it, nothing to install, and it works with the wifi off.
Step 2 — Open it in Google Chrome
WindowsRight-click the file → Open with → Google Chrome. Then tick Always use this app.
macOSRight-click → Open With → Google Chrome. Or drag the file onto the Chrome icon in the Dock.
Linuxgoogle-chrome ~/Documents/'JBS Praxis'/PRAXIS_ENGINEERING_WORKBOOK.html
CheckThe address bar should read file:///…. That is correct — this file is not served from anywhere.
Chrome or Edge, and not a private window. The workbook is built and tested against Chromium browsers; the PDF export in particular depends on how Chrome renders. Safari and Firefox will display the pages, but the export is untested there. Never use Incognito or Private mode — that storage is destroyed the moment you close the window, and a month of work goes with it.
Step 3 — Enrol
  • On first open you are asked for your full name. Type it as you want it to appear on a certificate, because that is exactly where it goes — spelling, capitals and all.
  • Your name is stored on your own machine only. Nothing is uploaded, there is no account, no login, no server. Open DevTools and watch the Network tab if you want to confirm that: the file makes zero requests.
  • After that, everything you do is recorded automatically as you go. There is no save button.
You need a working machine too, but not yet. Docker, Node, Git and an editor are Chapter 2's job, and that chapter installs them with you step by step, checking each one before moving on. Right now all you need is this file and Chrome.

// Protecting Your Work

The workbook remembers everything you do, automatically, with no save button. That is a convenience with one sharp edge: the memory lives in the browser, not in the file. Five things destroy it, and one habit protects you from all five.

Know how to protect your work
What is savedEvery checkbox, every typed answer, every self-check, which pages you have read, and your exam scores.
WhereChrome's localStorage, under one key: jbs-praxis-workbook-v1.
What destroys itReset in the top bar (it asks first) · clearing browsing data with Cookies and other site data ticked · Incognito · a different browser or profile · moving the file.
Your backupHit Download PDF at the end of each week. The export captures your typed answers and ticks as they stand, which makes it a snapshot you can keep or send to your lead.
What the top bar does
Download PDFExports the whole workbook — or just the pages you tick with the INCLUDE box — as a real PDF. Give it a minute; it renders every page at high resolution.
EditMakes every page directly editable. Correct a line, paste in a note from your lead, then export. Click again to lock it.
ResetWipes everything and starts you over, name included. It asks first. Nothing else in the workbook clears your data.
ProgressThe live percentage, and the teal bar along the bottom edge of the window.
Your nameShown on the right once you have enrolled, so you always know whose copy this is.
Export at the end of every week. It takes a minute and it is the only copy of your work that exists outside one browser profile on one machine. Engineers who lose three weeks of answers always lose them the same way: a routine clear-browsing-data, on a Friday, with the box ticked.
SELF-CHECK 0.1You have worked through Week 1. Tonight you clear your browsing history, including cookies and other site data, and reopen the workbook tomorrow. What do you find?
Why: The HTML file on disk never changes — your progress lives in the browser's localStorage for that file, not in the file. Clearing site data deletes it, permanently and without warning. This is exactly why the weekly PDF export exists: it is the only copy of your work that survives outside the browser.

// The Promise, and the Proof

At the end of four weeks you will not “know about” full-stack engineering. You will have shipped a working vertical slice into a system of real size, passed the same gates a senior engineer passes, and be able to do it again unaided.

The capability contract
  • 1Build a complete backend module — routes, validator, controller, service, repo, rules, events, AI manifest — that auto-mounts with no central wiring edit.
  • 2Write a migration that passes numbering, reversibility, idempotency and destructive-declaration checks.
  • 3Build the frontend for it: a list screen, a write form on a shared Zod schema, registered in the screen registry and the nav.
  • 4Make it multi-tenant safe — the right tenant, the right permission, one pooled connection, one transaction boundary.
  • 5Make it observable — events, audit rows, a correct error envelope with a request_id that survives to the client.
  • 6Give it an AI surface that obeys the same RBAC as the HTTP surface, and prove it cannot exceed it.
  • 7Take it through CI, review, deploy and rollback — 33 gates, branch protection, four containers, a one-shot migrate.
  • 8Train a client on it — the eight-step tenant go-live, sandbox seeding, and the incident runbook when it goes wrong at 2am.
  • 9Direct AI coding agents — Claude Code, Arena, Jules — to do this work faster than you could alone, and verify their output rather than trusting it.
The proof is a pull request. Week 4 ends with you opening a real PR against a real repository: a feature nobody has built, passing every gate, reviewed by a human who did not write it. That PR is the real graduation. The written examination at the back of this workbook — twenty questions, 80% to pass, a certificate in your name — only checks that you can explain what you built and why it is shaped that way.
Who this is for
  • The data engineer who writes good SQL and Python but has never owned an HTTP request end to end. You are the primary reader; the ramp is built for you.
  • The junior full-stack engineer who can build a CRUD app but has never worked in a codebase with 1,422 routes and cannot yet see why the discipline exists.
  • The experienced engineer joining JBS Praxis who needs the house conventions fast. Read chapters 1, 4, 7 and 11, run the labs, skip the rest.
SELF-CHECK 0.2Read the nine points above once more. Which statement is the most accurate description of what this workbook is asking of you?
Why: Every one of the nine points ends in something that exists after you have finished: a module, a migration, a screen, a deploy, a trained client. None of them ends in having read. The proof at the end of the month is a pull request against a real repository, reviewed by somebody who did not write it — which is also why the labs are not optional and not done on a private copy.

01
The Shape of the System
WEEK 1 · TEACH · ~3 HOURS · NO CODE YET

Before you change one line, you need a map. A codebase of this size punishes people who start typing early — not because it is clever, but because almost every rule in it was written the day something broke. This chapter is the map, and every claim in it points at a file you can open.

What you are looking at the numbers, so the scale is not a surprise
DimensionCountWhat that means for you
Backend JS files1,225You will never read them all. You will learn where to look.
Feature modules131 in 26 groupsEach is 5–8 small files in one folder. That is the unit of work.
HTTP routes1,422 (129 mounted)Auto-discovered. Nobody maintains a central route list.
Migrations313The schema's history, in order, forward-only in production.
Test files375Unit, integration, db and security gates.
Error codes478Generated into doc/ERROR_CODES.md, never hand-written.
Env vars86Every one validated by Zod at boot, or the process refuses to start.
CI gates33npm run ci. All must pass. There is no override.
None of this is here to intimidate you. A 131-module system is easier to work in than a 12-module one, provided every module has the same shape. That is the whole bet this codebase makes: relentless sameness, so that knowing one module means knowing all of them. Chapter 3 teaches you that one module.
The one-sentence description
Praxis LS is a multi-tenant ERP platform: one Node/Express API and one React SPA, serving many client companies whose data is separated by Postgres schema, with a background worker fleet, a Redis-backed queue, and an AI layer that can drive the same operations a user can — under exactly the same permissions.
SELF-CHECK 1.1Why does the number of routes (1,422) matter more than the number of files (1,225)?
Why: Files are an implementation detail you can reorganise freely. A route is a published contract: a client's browser, a mobile app or an integration may be calling it right now. That is why this repo has an API-contract gate in CI and generates doc/API_REFERENCE.md from the code rather than by hand.
CHAPTER 1 — THE SHAPE OF THE SYSTEM  ·  ORIENTATION
09

// The Five Layers

Everything in src/ belongs to exactly one of five layers, and the layers only ever call downward. If you can place a file in this list, you know what it is allowed to do.

1 · Entry
src/server.js, src/routes/index.js		Builds the Express app, applies global middleware, mounts two API surfaces: /api/platform/* (JBS staff) and /api/tenant/* (client users). Also serves the built SPA.
2 · Middleware
src/middleware/		Twelve files, each answering one question about a request before a handler sees it: who is the tenant, who is the user, may they do this, is this a replay, what is the request id.
3 · Modules
src/modules/<group>/<module>/		The features. 131 folders, each with the same file set. This is where you will spend 80% of your time.
4 · Shared
src/shared/		The machinery modules stand on: db helpers, transactions, the CRUD factory, event emission, HTTP utilities, cache, observability. Changing something here changes 131 modules at once, so it is the most carefully guarded code in the repo.
5 · Services & Jobs
src/services/, src/jobs/		Cross-cutting concerns (AI, storage, mail, tenant registry) and everything that happens off the request thread: 44 queue handlers and their schedulers.
The rule that makes it work one direction only
A layer may call downward. It may never call upward, and it may never reach sideways past its own boundary. A controller does not run SQL. A repo does not emit events. A module does not import another module's repo. When you are unsure whether something belongs in the service or the repo, ask which layer would have to know about HTTP to make it work — that is always the wrong layer.
Where the other top-level directories live
  • src/config/ — env parsing (Zod), logger, Redis, request context. Boot-time only.
  • src/orchestration/ — multi-step processes that span modules.
  • src/realtime/ — websocket push.
  • src/utils/ — leaf helpers with no dependencies, including AppError.
  • client/ — the tenant React SPA. console/ — the JBS staff console. packages/ — brand tokens and schemas shared between server and client.
SELF-CHECK 1.2You need to send an email when an invoice is approved. Which layer owns that call?
Why: Business consequences belong to the service, but the service does not send the mail itself — it emits an event. Sending happens off the request thread in a job handler, so a slow or failing SMTP server cannot make an invoice approval time out. Putting it in the repo would tie mail delivery to a transaction that might roll back; putting it in the controller means it never happens when the same service is called from a job or the AI layer.
CHAPTER 1 — THE SHAPE OF THE SYSTEM  ·  THE FIVE LAYERS
10

// The Life of a Request

This is the single most valuable page in Chapter 1. Follow one HTTP call from the socket to the database and back. Every stage here is real, in order, and readable in src/server.js and src/routes/index.js.

# The request we are going to trace
POST https://acme.praxis.app/api/tenant/leads
Content-Type: application/json
Idempotency-Key: 6f1e-...
Cookie: session=...

{ "company_name": "Northwind Ltd", "contact_email": "ada@northwind.example" }
Stage by stage
  • 01helmet, compression, cors — security headers, gzip, and the origin allowlist. The allowlist reflects any host on APP_BASE_DOMAIN, plus exact entries in CORS_ORIGINS, plus localhost in dev only.
  • 02requestIdMiddleware — attaches a request_id. It appears in every log line, in the error envelope, and in the audit row. When a client reports a bug, this is the only string you need.
  • 03buildAccessLog() — one structured line per request: who called what, with what outcome. Note that it is mounted after request-id, so the id is in the log.
  • 04express.json({ limit: "2mb" }) — body parsing, with a cap. A missing limit is a denial-of-service..
  • 05apiVersionHeaders then apiLimiter — version advertisement, then rate limiting backed by Redis so limits are shared across every API container, not per-process.
  • 06hostTenantResolver — reads the Host header, finds the tenant. acme.praxis.app → tenant acme. Platform hosts (localhost, api.*, admin.*, the apex) deliberately set no tenant.
  • 07tenantContext — picks live vs sandbox, binds the ambient request context, and exposes req.tenantDb(fn): a lazily acquired, once-per-request pooled connection with the tenant's search_path already set.
  • 08idempotency — mounted above the module loader so all ~700 tenant write endpoints get replay protection without opting in. No Idempotency-Key header means straight through, unchanged.
  • 09mountTenantModules — the auto-discovered module router matches /leads and hands off to sales/lead/lead.routes.js.
  • 10Per-route chain — authMiddleware → requirePermission(MODULE, "create") → validator.create → controller.create.
  • 11Controller → service → repo — the controller unwraps HTTP, the service applies rules and emits events, the repo runs the only SQL in the building.
  • 12Response, or errorHandler — success returns the mutation envelope; any thrown error becomes { error: { code, message, fields }, request_id } with the right status.
Read stage 06 and 07 again. Tenant isolation in this system is not a WHERE tenant_id = ? that a developer might forget. It is a Postgres search_path bound to a connection before your code runs. You physically cannot query another tenant's table from a request handler, because the schema those tables live in is not on your path.
CHAPTER 1 — THE SHAPE OF THE SYSTEM  ·  THE LIFE OF A REQUEST
11

// Multi-Tenancy, Concretely

“Multi-tenant” is the word that most often hides a security incident. Here is exactly what it means in this repo, with the three things that will bite you.

The model schema-per-tenant
One databasePostgres, with the pgvector extension for AI embeddings.
One schema per tenantClient Acme's tables live in schema acme; Northwind's in northwind. Same table names, same columns, different schema.
A platform schemaJBS-owned data: the tenant registry, error events, feature flags. Not reachable from a tenant request.
Sandbox schemasA non-live tenant can carry a parallel sandbox schema, selected with the X-Praxis-Env: sandbox header, for training and demos (Chapter 13).
The three things that will bite you
TRAP 1
THE CONNECTION IS SHARED
  • One request = one connection, on purpose
  • Two req.tenantDb calls are NOT isolated from each other
  • Never Promise.all over req.tenantDb
TRAP 2
THE WRONG HOST
  • localhost is a platform host, not a tenant host
  • Tenant calls from it get 400 WRONG_HOST
  • In dev, send X-Praxis-Tenant: <slug>
TRAP 3
IDENTIFIERS ARE NOT VALUES
  • A schema or column name can't be a bind parameter
  • Use ident() from shared/db/query-helpers.js
  • Chapter 4 covers the three-layer defence
The wrong-host trap is a teaching example in itself. It used to answer 500. A misaddressed request is a client error, and answering 500 told the caller the server was broken when their Host header was. It now returns 400 WRONG_HOST with a message that names the fix. Read the comment in src/middleware/tenant-context.js — this repo documents why, not what, and you are expected to write comments to that standard.
SELF-CHECK 1.3A colleague writes await Promise.all([req.tenantDb(a), req.tenantDb(b)]) to speed up a handler. What happens?
Why: Since PERF-S2 the request holds a single lazily-acquired client. pg serialises statements on one client, so there is no parallelism to win, and the two calls are no longer isolated from one another. The performance comment in tenant-context.js states that nothing in src/ does this, and it must stay that way.
CHAPTER 1 — THE SHAPE OF THE SYSTEM  ·  MULTI-TENANCY
12

// Why Nobody Edits a Route Table

In most codebases, adding a feature means editing a central file that everyone else is also editing. Here, the router finds you. Understanding this one mechanism explains half the conventions in Chapter 3.

What the loader does src/shared/http/module-loader.js
  • 1Walks src/modules/ looking for two layouts: nested <group>/<module>/<module>.routes.js, or flat <module>/<module>.routes.js for a standalone module.
  • 2A directory that contains module subfolders is treated as a group, and its own .routes.js is ignored. platform is skipped entirely — it mounts separately, with its own auth.
  • 3Folder names must match ^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*$. snake_case, always. A folder named myModule is invisible to the loader — and this is the most common reason a new engineer's first route 404s.
  • 4Each routes file must export { basePath, feature, router }. The loader mounts router at basePath, wrapped in requireFeature(feature) when feature is non-null.
  • 5A module whose require() throws is skipped with a warning, not fatal. One broken module cannot stop the server booting — which is why the wiring gates in tests/security/ exist to catch what the warning would otherwise hide.
# The contract, from the bottom of every routes file
module.exports = { basePath: "/leads", feature: null, router };

# basePath  the URL under /api/tenant — here /api/tenant/leads
# feature   a feature-flag key, or null for always-on
# router    an express.Router()
“Skipped with a warning” is the single most dangerous behaviour in the loader, and the repo knows it. A module that fails to load produces a log line nobody reads, a route that 404s, and a green test suite. That is exactly the shape of the “declared, not called” family of defects catalogued in this codebase — and why tests/security/orphan-wiring-sweep.test.js exists to fail the build when a module stops mounting. A warning is not a gate.
Predict the URL5 min

Given a routes file at src/modules/procurement/purchase_order/purchase_order.routes.js exporting basePath: "/purchase-orders", write the full path a tenant browser would call, including the API prefix and version behaviour described on the request-life page.

SELF-CHECK 1.4You create src/modules/sales/quoteItem/quoteItem.routes.js and the route 404s. Why?
Why: The loader only descends into directories matching ^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*$. quoteItem contains an uppercase letter, so it is silently invisible — no error, no warning, just a 404. Rename to quote_item. This is a five-minute bug that has cost people an afternoon.

02
Environment & First Run
WEEK 1 · LAB · ~4 HOURS · TERMINAL OPEN

By the end of this chapter the whole platform runs on your machine: Postgres with pgvector, Redis, a connection pooler, the migrator, the API, the worker fleet, and both front ends. You will also run the 33-gate CI suite for the first time and read what it tells you.

The two ways to run it
OPTION A
DOCKER COMPOSE — RECOMMENDED
  • One command, everything included
  • Matches production topology exactly
  • Slower file watching on macOS
  • Start here on day one
OPTION B
NATIVE — FASTER INNER LOOP
  • You install Postgres 16 + Redis yourself
  • npm run setup:local does the rest
  • Fastest edit-reload cycle
  • Move here once Option A has worked once
Do Option A first, even if you intend to live in Option B. Getting the compose stack up proves your Docker, your ports and your .env are sane, and it is the same topology you will deploy in Chapter 11. Debugging a native setup without ever having seen the system work is the hard way round.
The services, and what each is for
postgresPostgres 16 on the stock pgvector image. Holds every tenant schema plus platform. The vector extension is for AI embeddings (Chapter 9), not an optional extra.
redisThree jobs: the BullMQ queue backing src/jobs/, the shared rate-limit store, and the cache in src/shared/cache/.
pgbouncerConnection pooler. Postgres connections are expensive; with several API containers plus a worker fleet you exhaust max_connections quickly. The pooler is why the app can scale horizontally.
migrateA one-shot container. Runs platform then tenant migrations and exits. Deploys wait for it to exit 0 before starting the app — that ordering is the whole point.
api / api-standbynode src/server.js. Two of them, so a deploy can shift traffic without a gap.
workernode src/jobs/workers.js. Consumes the queue: PDF rendering, email, FX sync, mail sync, sweeps.
uptime-probePolls the health endpoints and records availability. Chapter 11.
puppeteer-preflightVerifies the headless-Chrome dependency needed for PDF rendering, at startup rather than at 2am when a client asks for an invoice.
SELF-CHECK 2.1Why is migrate a separate one-shot container instead of code that runs when the API boots?
Why: If each API container migrated on boot, three containers would race to apply the same migration, and a container could serve requests against a half-migrated schema. A one-shot container that must exit 0 first gives you a single, ordered, verifiable migration step — the same reason the deploy script waits on it.
CHAPTER 2 — ENVIRONMENT & FIRST RUN  ·  WHAT YOU ARE BUILDING
17

// 86 Variables, and Why It Refuses To Boot

.env.example is 21 KB and defines 86 variables. That sounds hostile until you understand the design: every one is parsed and validated by Zod at boot, and a missing or malformed value stops the process rather than producing a subtle runtime failure three hours later.

Fail fast, loudly src/config/env.js
A misconfigured system that boots is worse than one that doesn't. If SMTP_HOST is empty and the app starts anyway, you discover it when a client's password-reset email never arrives — silently, days later, with no error anywhere. Validating at boot converts an invisible production incident into a visible startup failure on your laptop. This is the same instinct as the CI gates: move the failure as early and as loudly as possible.
The groups
GroupExamplesNote
CoreNODE_ENV, PORT, APP_BASE_DOMAINAPP_BASE_DOMAIN drives tenant resolution and the CORS allowlist.
AuthJWT_SECRET, session config, TRUST_PROXY_HOPSTRUST_PROXY_HOPS is a security control — see below.
DatabaseDATABASE_URL, pool sizes, statement timeoutsPool max interacts with the one-connection-per-request model.
RedisREDIS_URL, queue prefixesShared by queue, cache and rate limiter.
AIVendor keys, model names, embedding configChapter 9. Absent keys degrade features, they do not crash.
MailSMTP_*, IMAP sync settingsThe mail module both sends and syncs.
StorageDriver (local or s3), bucket, signing TTLThe /media route is allow-listed regardless of driver.
OpsAlerting webhooks, health thresholds, backup and restore-drill schedules, uptime, DB budgetChapter 11 uses all of these.
One variable worth studying
# src/server.js
app.set("trust proxy", config.TRUST_PROXY_HOPS > 0 ? config.TRUST_PROXY_HOPS : false);
  • This was once true, meaning “trust the entire X-Forwarded-For chain”.
  • The left of that chain is written by the client. So req.ip was attacker-controlled.
  • Which meant every IP-keyed rate limiter could be bypassed, and every audit row's ip could be forged.
  • A hop count makes Express take the address appended by the proxy you actually run.
Notice the shape of that fix. The vulnerable version was not sloppy — trust proxy: true is in a hundred tutorials. It was wrong for this deployment. Most real security work looks like this: not exotic exploits, but a default that stops being safe once you know where your traffic comes from.

// Lab 2A — Bringing It Up

Paste the output of docker compose ps. For each service, note its state. Then answer: which one is not running, and why is that correct?

Step 4 — Prove it is alive
curl -s localhost:3000/api/health          # liveness  — must never fail
curl -s localhost:3000/api/health/ready    # readiness — probes PG, Redis, modules
Two health endpoints, not one, and the difference is a real lesson. Liveness answers “is the process alive” and has no dependencies, so it cannot fail. Readiness actually probes Postgres, Redis and the module loader, and returns 503 when they are down. There used to be a single inline {ok:true} handler, and deploy.sh used it as the gate that said a deploy had worked — a check that could not fail, guarding the thing most worth checking. Chapter 11 returns to this.
SELF-CHECK 2.2/api/health returns 200 but /api/health/ready returns 503. What have you learned?
Why: That is precisely the split the two endpoints exist to express. An orchestrator uses liveness to decide whether to restart the container and readiness to decide whether to route traffic to it. Restarting on a failed readiness probe when the real problem is that Postgres is down turns one outage into a crash loop.

SELF-CHECK 2.3npm run lint is configured as eslint . --max-warnings 136. Why an oddly specific number?
Why: A ratchet is how you improve a large codebase without stopping to fix everything first. Zero would fail today; unlimited permits infinite decay. Pinning the current count means any new warning fails the build, and every cleanup PR lowers the number. You will meet the same pattern as a coverage ratchet in Chapter 6.

Reading a Module
WEEK 1 · TEACH · ~4 HOURS · THE MOST IMPORTANT CHAPTER

131 modules, one shape. This chapter dissects the canonical example — src/modules/sales/lead/ — file by file, line by line. Learn this folder and you can read any of the other 130. It is roughly 450 lines in total, and every one of them is teaching something.

The file set
FileLinesJobMay it…
lead.routes.js42URL → middleware chain → controllertouch SQL? No
lead.validator.js105Zod schemas + Express middlewaretouch SQL? No
lead.controller.js30Unwrap HTTP, call service, shape responsetouch SQL? No
lead.service.js192Business rules, transactions, events, audittouch SQL? No
lead.repo.js57Every SQL statement in the moduletouch SQL? Only here

lead.ai.js17The AI manifest — what the copilot may dotouch SQL? No
Notice the line counts. The controller is 30 lines for six endpoints. The rules file is 9. The events file is 3. This is not a codebase of clever abstractions — it is a codebase of tiny files with unambiguous jobs. When your controller starts growing, that is the signal that logic has leaked into the wrong layer.
How the layers call each other
STEP 1
ROUTES
auth → permission → validator → controller
STEP 2
CONTROLLER
reads req, calls req.tenantDb, calls the service
STEP 3
SERVICE
rules, transaction, repo calls, emitEvent, audit
STEP 4
REPO
parameterised SQL through the shared query helpers
SELF-CHECK 3.1Why does lead.rules.js exist as a separate 9-line file rather than living inside the service?
Why: Purity is the point. assertTransition(from, to) needs no database, no request and no mocks, so its test is instant and cannot rot. Everything genuinely hard about the module — ordering, transactions, side effects — stays in the service where it is visible, and the state machine stays somewhere you can read in ten seconds.
CHAPTER 3 — READING A MODULE  ·  THE EIGHT FILES
25

// File 1 — lead.routes.js

42 lines that define the module's entire public surface. Read the order of the middleware carefully: in Express, order is the security model.

const MODULE = "MOD-20";
const TRANSITION_ACTION = { CONTACTED: "edit", QUALIFIED: "edit", LOST: "approve" };

const router = express.Router();
router.use(authMiddleware);

router.get("/",            requirePermission(MODULE, "view"),   controller.list);
router.get("/:id/360",     requirePermission(MODULE, "view"),   controller.dossier);
router.get("/:id",         requirePermission(MODULE, "view"),   controller.get);
router.post("/",           requirePermission(MODULE, "create"), validator.create,  controller.create);

router.patch("/:id",       requirePermission(MODULE, "edit"),   validator.update,
  requireLifecyclePermissionOnPatch(MODULE, TRANSITION_ACTION, { field: "status" }), controller.update);

router.post("/:id/transition", validator.transition,
  requireTransitionPermission(MODULE, TRANSITION_ACTION), controller.transition);

router.post("/:id/convert", requirePermission(MODULE, "edit"), validator.convert, controller.convert);

module.exports = { basePath: "/leads", feature: null, router };
Four things to take from this file
  • AA module key, not a string per route. MOD-20 is the identity the permission system, the event system and the AI manifest all share. One constant, four subsystems.
  • BPermissions are per-action, not per-module. view, create, edit, approve. An administrator reading the permission matrix can see exactly what a role can do.
  • CThe transition map is the interesting part. This lifecycle used to be gated by one flat permission for every target state, so “advance this lead” and “kill this lead” required the same grant. Advancing is edit; a decision that ends the record is approve.
  • DAnything not listed falls back to approve. Read that again. A state added later, by someone who forgets this map, fails closed — it demands the higher permission rather than the lower one.
“Fail closed” is the single most transferable idea in this chapter. When a future developer extends an enum and forgets the permission table, the system must become more restrictive, not less. Design every lookup table you write so that the missing case is the safe case. You will apply this again in Chapters 8 and 9.
And one subtlety about ordering
  • On PATCH /:id, the flat edit permission runs first, then the validator, then the lifecycle check.
  • On POST /:id/transition, the validator runs first — deliberately. The target state must be checked against the enum before the permission middleware uses that state to select which gate to apply.
  • Otherwise a caller could send an unknown state and influence which permission was checked. That is the whole reason for the comment in the file.
SELF-CHECK 3.2Why does PATCH /:id need requireLifecyclePermissionOnPatch in addition to requirePermission(MODULE, "edit")?
Why: This is finding API F-17 in the repo. Deriving the update schema from the create schema is convenient and correct-looking, but it silently exposed every lifecycle field to a route gated only by edit. The extra middleware applies the same gate as /transition — but only when the body actually carries the field.
CHAPTER 3 — READING A MODULE  ·  FILE 1 — ROUTES
26

// File 2 — lead.validator.js

105 lines, and the largest file after the service. That ratio is intentional: this is the boundary where untrusted input becomes trusted data, and it is worth being verbose about.

const schemas = {
  create: z.object({
    company_name: z.string().min(1),
    email: z.string().email().optional(),
    payment_terms_days: z.number().int().min(0).max(365).optional().nullable(),
    client_type_hint: z.enum(CLIENT_TYPE).optional().nullable(),
    /* … */
  }),
  update: z.object({ /* … */ }),
  transition: z.object({ to: z.enum(["CONTACTED", "QUALIFIED", "LOST"]) }),
  convert: z.object({ client: z.object({ client_type: z.enum(CLIENT_TYPE),
                                          payment_terms_days: z.number().int().min(0).max(365) }) }),
  aiTransition: z.object({ lead_id: z.string().uuid(), to: z.enum([...]) }),
  aiConvert:    z.object({ lead_id: z.string().uuid(), client: z.object({ … }) }),
};

const mw = (k) => (req, _res, next) => {
  const p = schemas[k].safeParse(req.body);
  if (!p.success) return next(new AppError("VALIDATION_ERROR", "Invalid body", 422, p.error.flatten().fieldErrors));
  req.body = p.data;   // ← the parsed value replaces the raw one
  return next();
};
The five lessons in that middleware factory
  • 1safeParse, not parse. No exception to catch; an explicit branch you can shape into the house error envelope.
  • 2422, not 400. The body was well-formed JSON but semantically invalid. The distinction matters to clients that retry.
  • 3fieldErrors is passed through. That is what lets the front end highlight the offending input rather than showing one generic toast. The error envelope's fields key exists for exactly this.
  • 4req.body = p.data. Downstream code sees the parsed object — coerced, stripped of unknown keys, type-safe. Nothing after this line touches raw input.
  • 5Schemas are exported, not just the middleware. module.exports = { create: mw("create"), …, schemas, INTAKE_CHANNEL, CLIENT_TYPE }.
Lesson 5 is why the AI layer is safe. lead.ai.js imports validator.schemas.aiTransition and hands it to the action registry. The copilot's input is validated by the same Zod object as the HTTP path — not a parallel schema someone has to remember to update. One definition, two front doors. Chapter 9 builds on this.
Why there are separate ai* variants
  • REST takes the id from the URL: POST /leads/:id/transition with body { to }.
  • The AI action has no URL, so the id must be in the payload: { lead_id, to }.
  • Hence aiTransition = transition + lead_id: z.string().uuid().
  • The comment notes that lead_id resolves to a list_leads picker in the copilot form — the schema drives the UI too.
SELF-CHECK 3.3A teammate adds a field to create but forgets update. What is the practical consequence?
Why: The two schemas are written out separately in this module, which is explicit and readable but does allow exactly this drift. It is the trade-off against create.partial() — which caused API F-17 by making everything patchable. There is no free option here; the answer is a test that exercises both paths.
CHAPTER 3 — READING A MODULE  ·  FILE 2 — VALIDATOR
27

// File 3 — lead.controller.js

Thirty lines for six endpoints. Most handlers are a single expression. This is what a controller should look like when the layering is honest.

const actor = (req) => req.user || { user_id: null };

list: asyncHandler(async (req, res) =>
  res.json({ data: await req.tenantDb((c) => service.list(c, req.query)) })),

get: asyncHandler(async (req, res) => {
  const r = await req.tenantDb((c) => service.get(c, req.params.id));
  if (!r) throw new AppError("NOT_FOUND", "Lead not found", 404);
  res.json({ data: r });
}),

create: asyncHandler(async (req, res) =>
  res.status(201).json({ data: await req.tenantDb((c) =>
    service.create(c, { data: req.body, actor: actor(req) })) })),
What the controller is responsible for, exactly
Acquiring the connectionreq.tenantDb(c => …). The controller owns the connection scope; the service receives a client and never knows where it came from.
Translating ‘nothing found’The service returns null; the controller turns that into 404. HTTP semantics live at the HTTP layer.
Choosing the status code201 for create, 200 for the rest.
Shaping the envelopeEverything comes back as { data: … }. Consistency is what makes a generic client possible.
Identifying the actorreq.user || { user_id: null }, passed down so the service can write audit rows.
asyncHandler, and why it is not optional
Express 4 does not catch rejected promises from an async handler. Without a wrapper, a thrown error inside async (req,res) becomes an unhandled rejection — the request hangs until it times out, and in some Node versions the process dies. Every handler here is wrapped. The repo also loads shared/http/async-safe as the very first line of server.js, as a belt-and-braces backstop, precisely because forgetting the wrapper is so easy.
The dossier endpoint, and a rule about money
dossier: asyncHandler(async (req, res) => {
  const canSee = await canSeeFinancials(req);
  res.json({ data: await req.tenantDb((c) =>
    sales360.leadDossier(c, { leadId: req.params.id, canSeeFinancials: canSee })) });
}),
  • The route gates this on view, because the dossier aggregates records the caller can already open one screen at a time.
  • But money is gated separately, on the same finance-visibility check the party masters use — not a second rule invented here.
  • And hidden money comes back as null, not zero. Zero is a fact; null is an absence. Showing a pipeline value of 0 to someone who is not allowed to see it is a lie the UI will happily total up.
SELF-CHECK 3.4Why does the controller call canSeeFinancials(req) instead of the service doing it?
Why: This is the layering rule doing real work. Anything derived from req is resolved at the HTTP boundary and passed down as a plain value. If the service reached for req, it would break the moment a queue handler or the copilot called it — and those callers are exactly where a forgotten permission becomes a data leak.
CHAPTER 3 — READING A MODULE  ·  FILE 3 — CONTROLLER
28

// File 4 — lead.service.js

192 lines, the biggest file in the module, and rightly so. This is where the business lives. Every line here is a decision someone had to make about how the business actually works.

async function create(client, { data, actor = {} }) {
  return atomically(client, async () => {
    const row = await repo.insert(client, {
      company_name: data.company_name,
      source: data.source || "MANUAL",
      intake_channel: data.intake_channel || data.source || "MANUAL",
      status: "NEW",
      owner_user_id: data.owner_user_id || actor.user_id || null,
      details_json: JSON.stringify(data.details || {}),
      /* … */
    });
    await emitEvent(client, { eventTypeKey: events.CREATED, moduleKey: events.MODULE,
                              entityRef: ref(row.lead_id), actorUserId: actor.user_id || null });
    await audit(client, { actorUserId: actor.user_id || null, action: events.CREATED,
                          moduleKey: events.MODULE, entityRef: ref(row.lead_id), after: row });
    return row;
  });
}
The anatomy of a write
  • 1Wrap in atomically. The row, the event and the audit entry commit together or not at all. An audit row for a lead that does not exist is worse than no audit row.
  • 2Defaults are explicit and visible. status: "NEW", source || "MANUAL". Read in one place, not scattered as column defaults in a migration.
  • 3Ownership falls back to the actor. data.owner_user_id || actor.user_id || null — you own what you create unless you say otherwise.
  • 4Emit an event, then audit. Two different things: the event drives downstream behaviour, the audit row is the permanent record of who did what.
  • 5Return the row. The controller wraps it; the service does not know about HTTP.
CHAPTER 3 — READING A MODULE  ·  FILE 4 — SERVICE
29

// The State Machine, Enforced

Nine lines in a separate file, and two independent checks that use them.

// lead.rules.js — the entire file
const NEXT = { NEW:       ["CONTACTED", "LOST"],
               CONTACTED: ["QUALIFIED", "LOST"],
               QUALIFIED: ["CONVERTED", "LOST"],
               CONVERTED: [], LOST: [] };

function assertTransition(from, to) {
  if (!NEXT[from] || !NEXT[from].includes(to))
    throw new AppError("BAD_STATE", `Cannot move lead ${from} -> ${to}`, 422);
  return true;
}
  • CONVERTED and LOST are terminal — empty arrays. Not a comment saying so; a structure that makes it impossible.
  • update() enforces the same idea separately: editing a CONVERTED or LOST lead throws LOCKED with 422.
  • Both checks read before from the repo first. The rule is applied to the row's actual current state, never to a state the client claimed.
Never trust the client's idea of the current state. A client that sends { from: "NEW", to: "CONVERTED" } is telling you what it believes, possibly from a stale page open since this morning. The service reads the row, then judges. This is also, incidentally, how you avoid a whole class of race condition.
SELF-CHECK 3.5update() throws LOCKED (422) for a CONVERTED lead. Why not 403?
Why: Status codes are diagnostic instructions to whoever reads the log at 2am. 403 says “this user lacks a grant” and sends someone to the permission matrix. 422 with LOCKED says “the request was understood and refused on business grounds”. Choosing the code that points at the real cause is a recurring theme — you saw it with WRONG_HOST and the CORS 403.
CHAPTER 3 — READING A MODULE  ·  FILE 4 — SERVICE (CONT.)
30

// File 5 — lead.repo.js

57 lines containing every SQL statement in the module. Small, boring, and the most security-sensitive file in the folder.

const { insertOne, getById, page, updateOne } = require("../../../shared/db/query-helpers");

const insert = (client, data) => insertOne(client, "lead", data);
const get    = (client, id)   => getById(client, "lead", "lead_id", id);

async function update(client, id, fields) {
  // PERF S19/S20: was a hand-rolled SET builder, which bypassed the
  // identifier validation and allow-list in query-helpers.
  if (!Object.keys(fields).length) return get(client, id);
  return updateOne(client, "lead", "lead_id", id, fields, "*", null, { touch: "updated_at" });
}
Read that comment again
“Was a hand-rolled SET builder, which bypassed the identifier validation and allow-list.” Someone wrote a perfectly reasonable UPDATE lead SET x = $1, y = $2 builder. It worked. It also constructed column names by string concatenation from an object whose keys came, ultimately, from a request body. The shared helper exists so that no module has to get this right individually — and the lesson is that the unsafe version looks completely normal.
The empty-patch guard
  • if (!Object.keys(fields).length) return get(client, id);
  • An UPDATE with no SET clause is a syntax error, so the naive version crashes on an empty patch.
  • Returning the current row is the honest answer to “change nothing”. It also means PATCH with an empty body is idempotent and harmless rather than a 500.
The list query, and the pagination helper
async function list(client, q = {}) {
  const { limit, offset } = page(q);
  const params = [limit, offset];
  const wh = [];
  if (q.status)       { params.push(q.status);       wh.push("status = $" + params.length); }
  if (q.owner_user_id){ params.push(q.owner_user_id);wh.push("owner_user_id = $" + params.length); }
  if (q.q)            { params.push("%" + q.q + "%");
                        wh.push("(company_name ILIKE $" + params.length + " OR …)"); }
  const where = wh.length ? "WHERE " + wh.join(" AND ") : "";
  const { rows } = await client.query(
    "SELECT * FROM lead " + where + " ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT $1 OFFSET $2", params);
  return rows;
}
  • The SQL string is concatenated, but no user value ever enters it. Only $n placeholders do. Values go in params. This is the distinction that matters — not “never build SQL with +”, but “never let a value become syntax”.
  • page(q) centralises limit/offset parsing, including the maximum page size. Without it, ?limit=1000000 is a denial-of-service.
  • ORDER BY created_at DESC is always present. An unordered paginated query returns arbitrary rows per page — Postgres makes no promise otherwise.
CHAPTER 3 — READING A MODULE  ·  FILE 5 — REPO
31

// The Repo's Two Lookup Helpers

Four lines of SQL each, and both exist because of something that went wrong.

clientTypeIdByCode() exists because of a 42703. client_master has a client_type_id FK and no client_type column. The convert path passed the code straight through to insertOne with a null allow-list — which puts every key into the INSERT column list verbatim. Postgres answered column client_type of relation client_master does not exist, conversion failed for every lead, and the unit test did not see it, because it mocks clientMaster.create.
That last clause is the lesson of Chapter 6, arriving early. A mock is an assumption about a boundary, written down. When the assumption is wrong, the mock does not just fail to catch the bug — it actively certifies the broken code as working. This is why this repo has a check-query-columns gate that verifies every queried column actually exists in the schema.
And a rule about defaults
// The tenant's default corporate entity, or null when genuinely ambiguous.
// One active entity is a default, two is a question. Never "the oldest" —
// that files a client, and its reference number, under the wrong company.
async function defaultEntityId(client) {
  const { rows } = await client.query(
    "SELECT entity_id FROM corporate_entity WHERE is_active IS NOT false LIMIT 2");
  return rows.length === 1 ? rows[0].entity_id : null;
}
“One is a default, two is a question.” Memorise that phrase. The tempting implementation is LIMIT 1, which always returns something and is always confidently wrong half the time. LIMIT 2 lets you distinguish “unambiguous” from “I must ask”. Note also is_active IS NOT false rather than = true — it treats NULL as active, which is what an un-backfilled column means.
CHAPTER 3 — READING A MODULE  ·  FILE 5 — REPO (CONT.)
32

// Files 6–8 — The Small Ones

Twenty-nine lines between them, and they connect this module to three whole subsystems.

lead.events.js — 3 lines
module.exports = { MODULE: "MOD-20",
  CREATED: "lead.created", UPDATED: "lead.updated", CONVERTED: "lead.converted",
  transition: (status) => "lead." + String(status).toLowerCase() };
  • Event names are constants, never string literals at the call site. A typo in "lead.creted" would emit an event nobody subscribes to — silently.
  • transition is a function, so lead.contacted, lead.qualified and lead.lost are generated rather than listed. Add a state and the event name follows for free.
  • MODULE lives here too, so the event system and the permission system agree on the module's identity by construction.
CHAPTER 3 — READING A MODULE  ·  FILES 6–8 — RULES, EVENTS, AI
33

// File 8 — lead.ai.js

Seventeen lines that connect this module to the copilot — and the single most important architectural idea in the repository.

module.exports = {
  entity: "lead", module_key: "MOD-20", screens: [],
  reads: [
    { key: "list_leads", service: (c, p) => service.list(c, p),
      permission: { module: "MOD-20", action: "view" },
      describe: "List sales leads (filter status/owner/intake_channel)." },
  ],
  writes: [
    { key: "transition_lead", service: (c, p) => service.transition(c, { id: p.lead_id, to: p.to }),
      schema: validator.schemas.aiTransition,
      permission: { module: "MOD-20", action: "edit" },
      confirm: true,
      describe: "Advance a lead by id to CONTACTED/QUALIFIED/LOST." },
  ],
};
Five properties, five guarantees
KeyGuarantee
serviceThe AI calls the same service function the HTTP controller calls. There is no parallel implementation to drift, and no way for the copilot to skip a business rule.
schemaThe same Zod schema validates the model's arguments. A hallucinated field is stripped; a malformed one is rejected before any code runs.
permissionThe same module/action pair as the REST route. The copilot can never do more than the logged-in user could do by hand.
confirmtrue on every write. The user is shown what is about to happen and must approve it. Reads do not ask.
describeThe natural-language description the model actually reads when choosing a tool. This is prompt engineering inside the codebase — Chapter 12 returns to it.
This is the most important architectural idea in the repo. The AI surface is not a new set of capabilities bolted on beside the application — it is a manifest over the capabilities that already exist, reusing their services, their schemas and their permissions. Every AI safety property follows from that one decision. Chapter 9 shows the registry that enforces it.
Read the descriptions as prompts15 min

Look at the describe strings above. convert_lead's says the client block MUST carry client_type and payment_terms_days, and that “the legacy's silent fallback to BOTH/30 is gone”. Why is that sentence in a field the model reads? What would happen if it just said “Convert a lead into a client”?

SELF-CHECK 3.6Could an engineer give the copilot a capability that no HTTP route exposes?
Why: The manifest is declarative, and a declaration is only as trustworthy as whatever validates it. That is why doc/CONVENTIONS.md is explicit that src/services/ai/action-registry.js is the safety boundary, and why an action also needs a row in ai_action_catalogue with a payload_schema. Two independent places must agree before the copilot can do anything.

You are a data engineer. This is the chapter where your existing skill is worth the most — and where the gap between “writes good SQL” and “writes good SQL inside a multi-tenant application” is widest. Five CI gates guard this layer. By the end you will know why each exists.

What is different here
In a data pipelineIn this application
You own the warehouse; you can rebuild it313 migrations of client data that can never be recreated
A failed job reruns tomorrowA failed migration blocks a deploy for every tenant at once

That last row is the one to sit with. In a pipeline, the SQL is written by you and reviewed by a human. In an application with generic CRUD helpers, part of the SQL — the column list — is built from a JavaScript object whose keys came from the internet. That single fact produced the most serious defect in this repo's history, and it is the first thing we look at.

CHAPTER 4 — DATA & MIGRATIONS  ·  THE DATABASE LAYER
37

// SEC H3: When The Comment Was The Bug

Open src/shared/db/query-helpers.js and read the header. It is the best security lesson in the codebase, and it starts by admitting that the previous version of itself lied.

The old header said: “Table/column names are always code-provided (never user input).” That was not true — and the assertion is why nobody looked.
How the untruth happened
  • 1insertOne and updateOne build their column list from Object.keys(data).
  • 2That is safe for a module with a Zod validator, because z.object strips unknown keys and the middleware reassigns req.body = p.data. So for 121 modules the claim held.
  • 3But ten modules were on passthrough — a pair of no-op middlewares. makeController.create/update handed req.body through untouched.
  • 4For those ten, the keys of an attacker's JSON body became the column list of a live SQL statement.
The two defects that followed
MASS ASSIGNMENT
ANY COLUMN WRITABLE
  • A holder of MOD-67 edit could clear killed_at on a revoked session
  • — resurrecting an admin session security staff believed they had terminated
  • Or repoint a session's user_id entirely
IDENTIFIER INJECTION
A KEY WAS SQL
  • Keys were concatenated with no quoting and no validation
  • So a key was a SQL fragment, not a name
  • Turning a tenant-admin grant into arbitrary SQL on the tenant database, under the shared application role
The fix: three layers, because any one alone leaves a gap
const IDENT_RE = /^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]{0,62}$/;

function ident(name, ctx) {
  if (typeof name !== "string" || !IDENT_RE.test(name)) {
    throw new AppError("INVALID_FIELD",
      `"${String(name).slice(0, 40)}" is not a valid column name`, 422,
      { [ctx || "body"]: [`unrecognised field "${String(name).slice(0, 40)}"`] });
  }
  return `"${name}"`;     // ← 2. quoted, AFTER being validated
}
  • L1Validate against a strict pattern and reject. This is what closes injection, and it cannot be forgotten by a module author because it lives here, not at 131 call sites.
  • L2Quote, so even a valid-but-reserved word behaves. Note the order: quoting alone is not sufficient, because a key containing a double quote would escape it. Pattern first, then quote, in one place that cannot be bypassed.
  • L3Allow-list — makeRepo may declare writable, which closes mass assignment independently of injection.
The regex is deliberately narrower than Postgres allows. No dollar signs, no unicode, no embedded quotes, 63 characters. Every column in this schema fits it. Anything that does not is either a mistake or an attack, and both should stop here. When you write a validator, validate against what your system actually uses, not against what the underlying technology permits.
SELF-CHECK 4.1Why does assertWritable reject a non-writable field instead of silently dropping it?
Why: Silent dropping produces the worst possible outcome: a 200 response describing a mutation that did not occur. The caller believes it worked. The comment names the precedent — “silent dropping is how F-16's unknown-filter bug went unnoticed for so long”. A filter that is silently ignored returns more rows than asked for, and looks like success.
CHAPTER 4 — DATA & MIGRATIONS  ·  SEC H3 — THE THREE-LAYER DEFENCE
38

// One Owner of the Transaction Boundary

src/shared/db/tx.js is 90 lines and solves a problem most codebases never notice they have. It exists because two Critical audit findings shared a root cause: nothing wrapped anything.

The findings
  • DATA 5.2 — the shared CRUD kit did not wrap its statements.
  • DATA 5.1 — nor did the inventory balance path.
  • And no controller wrapped them either. Verified: zero transaction( calls in any *.controller.js.
  • Consequence: a business row could commit while its audit entry did not. A stock balance could move with no movement record.
Why a shared helper, not BEGIN/COMMIT at each site
Postgres has no nested transactions. A second BEGIN inside an open transaction is a warning and a no-op — and then the inner COMMIT commits the outer transaction early. That is far worse than the bug being fixed: the caller believes it still holds a transaction it can roll back, and it does not.
Detecting that reliably needs one owner of the boundary. Every path that opens a transaction goes through atomically(), so the depth counter is always accurate. A nested call runs inline and lets the outermost caller decide the outcome — which is the semantics callers actually expect.
CHAPTER 4 — DATA & MIGRATIONS  ·  TRANSACTIONS
39

// The SAVEPOINT Probe

The depth counter only knows about transactions opened through the helper. Here is how it copes with the 76 that are not.

async function inForeignTransaction(client) {
  try {
    await client.query("SAVEPOINT praxis_tx_probe");
    await client.query("RELEASE SAVEPOINT praxis_tx_probe");
    return true;
  } catch {
    return false;   // 25P01 — "SAVEPOINT can only be used in transaction blocks"
  }
}
  • QThe problem: the depth counter only knows about transactions opened through here. There are 76 raw client.query("BEGIN") sites in src/. If one of those calls a function that uses this helper, the naive path breaks in exactly the way described above.
  • AThe probe: SAVEPOINT is only legal inside a transaction block. Outside one, Postgres raises 25P01. So attempting one is a reliable, one-round-trip test for “am I already inside someone else's transaction?” The savepoint is released immediately and changes nothing.
  • CThe cost: one round-trip on write paths that were already doing several. Worth it, because it makes the helper safe to call from anywhere — and that property is what lets the 76 raw sites be converted gradually rather than in one risky sweep.
That last point is a lesson about changing large systems. The pure fix is “convert all 76 sites” — one enormous, unreviewable, all-or-nothing pull request. Instead, the helper was made safe in the presence of the old pattern, so the migration can happen one site at a time, each independently reviewable and revertible. Design your fix so the transition can be incremental, and you will actually finish it.
Also note: a Symbol, not a string key
const DEPTH = Symbol.for("praxis.tx.depth");
  • Pooled clients are long-lived and shared across requests.
  • A string property like client.__txDepth risks collision with pg internals or another library.
  • Symbol.for keeps it in the global registry, so the same symbol resolves even across module instances.
SELF-CHECK 4.2Your service calls atomically() and inside it calls another service that also calls atomically(). What happens?
Why: Nested calls join the outer transaction. A throw anywhere propagates and the outermost handler rolls everything back — which is what a caller composing two services actually wants. The comment notes SAVEPOINTs would enable genuine partial rollback and are the right upgrade if a caller ever needs it; nothing does today, and a savepoint per nested call costs a round-trip each.
CHAPTER 4 — DATA & MIGRATIONS  ·  THE SAVEPOINT PROBE
40

// Migrations, and Their Five Gates

313 migrations, applied in order, to every tenant schema. Five separate CI gates check them before a human even reviews. Here is what each one wants from you.

GateScriptWhat it enforces
Numberingcheck-migration-numbers.jsFilenames carry a unique, ordered number. Two engineers cannot both claim 00314 and have the ordering depend on who merged first.
Reversibilitycheck-migration-reversibility.jsEvery migration declares how to undo itself — a -- DOWN block, even if only to state what would be lost.
Idempotencycheck-migration-idempotency.jsRe-running must not fail. IF NOT EXISTS, IF EXISTS, guarded inserts. Half-applied migrations happen, and the recovery path is to run it again.
Destructivecheck-destructive-migrations.jsA DROP, a TRUNCATE, a narrowing ALTER TYPE must be explicitly declared, so nobody deletes a column by accident during review.
Schema driftcheck-schema-drift.jsThe schema the migrations produce matches the schema the code expects. Paired with check-query-columns.js, which verifies every column named in a query exists.
check-query-columns.js is the gate that would have caught the client_type bug from Chapter 3. The convert path queried a column that did not exist; the unit test mocked the boundary and passed; production returned 42703 for every conversion. A gate that reads your SQL and checks the columns against the real schema catches that class of bug without needing anyone to write a test for it.
CHAPTER 4 — DATA & MIGRATIONS  ·  MIGRATIONS — FIVE GATES
41

// The Migration Workflow

Five gates, run in the order you will actually meet them.

# 1. Create the file. Numbering convention: check the highest existing number.
ls migrations/tenant/ | sort | tail -3

# 2. Write it (see the next page for the house prose style).

# 3. Apply locally
npm run db:migrate:platform      # platform schema
npm run db:migrate:tenants       # every tenant schema

# 4. Run the gates before you even think about a PR
node scripts/db/check-migration-numbers.js
node scripts/db/check-migration-reversibility.js
npm run db:check:idempotency
node scripts/db/check-destructive-migrations.js
npm run db:check:columns

# 5. Or just run them all
npm run ci:backend
Platform vs tenant migrations
migrations/platform/The JBS-owned schema: the tenant registry, error events, feature flags. Applied once.
migrations/tenant/The per-client schema. Applied to every tenant schema, including ones provisioned next year. Your migration must work on a brand-new empty schema and on a three-year-old one full of data.
SELF-CHECK 4.3Why must a tenant migration be idempotent when the migration runner already tracks which have been applied?
Why: Anything that can be interrupted — a killed container, a network partition, a statement timeout — can leave you between states. If re-running is safe, recovery is trivial and boring. If it is not, recovery is a human writing ad-hoc SQL against a client's production database at midnight, which is where real data loss comes from.
CHAPTER 4 — DATA & MIGRATIONS  ·  MIGRATIONS — THE WORKFLOW
42

// The House Migration Style

This is a JBS Praxis standard, and it is not optional. A migration is the one artefact that a stranger will read years later, under pressure, trying to work out whether they can undo it. Open migrations/tenant/12743_hr_contract_doc_number.sql — this is the model.

The five required sections
  • 1Banner comment — what this migration does, in one line.
  • 2WHAT WAS WRONG — the real symptom, not the abstract problem. In the example: contracts printed a document number derived as String(id).slice(0,8).
  • 3WHY A COLUMN AND NOT A DERIVATION — the alternative you rejected, and why. Here: a document number is allocated once and quoted in letters; deriving it renumbers the document on every render.
  • 4The nullability reasoning — why nullable with a partial unique index, rather than NOT NULL with a backfill. Because backfilling would invent a reference nobody was ever given.
  • 5COMMENT ON COLUMN, then a commented -- DOWN block stating exactly what is lost if you reverse it.
-- 00314_add_lead_score.sql
-- Adds a persisted lead score to the sales lead record.
--
-- WHAT WAS WRONG
--   The pipeline board sorted leads by a score computed in the browser from
--   whatever fields happened to be loaded. Two users with different column
--   sets saw different orderings of the same board, and neither ordering
--   survived a page refresh.
--
-- WHY A COLUMN AND NOT A DERIVATION
--   The score is an input to a human decision that gets recorded elsewhere
--   ("we prioritised this lead on Tuesday"). A derived score changes silently
--   when the formula changes, which rewrites the reason for a past decision.
--   Storing it means the score that drove a decision is still visible after
--   the model is retuned.
--
-- NULLABLE, NOT DEFAULTED
--   A lead scored before this column existed has no score, and 0 is not the
--   same as "unscored" — 0 would sort it to the bottom as though it had been
--   assessed and rejected. Nullable, and the board sorts NULLs last.

ALTER TABLE lead ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS score integer;

COMMENT ON COLUMN lead.score IS
  'Prioritisation score at the time of assessment. NULL = never scored. '
  'Deliberately persisted, not derived: see migration header.';

-- DOWN
--   ALTER TABLE lead DROP COLUMN score;
--   LOSES: every historical score, and therefore the ability to explain why
--   any past prioritisation decision was made. Not recoverable from backups
--   without a full restore.
The -- DOWN block is commented out on purpose. It is documentation of the reversal, not an executable rollback. Production is forward-only: you fix a bad migration with a new migration. The block exists so that the person considering the reversal knows the cost before they start — and “LOSES: …” is the most important line in the file.
Write the header before the SQL20 min

You are adding a closed_at timestamptz to a support ticket table. Write the WHAT WAS WRONG and WHY A COLUMN AND NOT A DERIVATION sections before writing any SQL. If you cannot fill in section 3 convincingly, that is a signal — say what it is a signal of.

The fastest way to trust a gate is to watch it catch you. You will deliberately write five bad migrations, confirm each gate fires, then throw them all away. Do this on a scratch branch and do not commit.

Setup

The five breakages
4.1Numbering

4.2Reversibility

Lab — Ship A Real Migration
WEEK 2 · HANDS ON · ~60 MIN · THIS ONE YOU KEEP

Chapter 5 builds a module, and that module needs a table. Write it now, to the house standard, and get it through all five gates. This is the first artefact of your graduation PR.

The feature
Onboarding Task. When a new client is signed, the team runs a checklist of onboarding tasks. Each task belongs to a client, has a title, an owner, a due date, a status (PENDING → IN_PROGRESS → DONE, or CANCELLED), and optional notes. This is a small, real, self-contained feature — and one this workbook's own subject matter cares about, since Chapter 13 is client onboarding.
Requirements
  • Table onboarding_task in the tenant schema.
  • A UUID primary key, defaulted — match the convention other tables use.
  • client_id referencing the client master, with a considered ON DELETE behaviour.
  • title text NOT NULL, with a check that it is not blank.
  • status with a default of PENDING and a constraint restricting it to the four values.
  • owner_user_id nullable — a task can exist before it is assigned.
  • due_date date nullable, notes text nullable.
  • created_at and updated_at, defaulted, matching the house pattern.
  • An index on the column your list screen will filter by most.
  • COMMENT ON the table and on at least two columns.
  • A full header with all five prose sections.
  • A commented -- DOWN block naming exactly what is lost.
Copy the conventions, do not invent them. Before writing a line, open three existing tenant migrations and note: how UUIDs are defaulted, how timestamps are named and defaulted, how check constraints are named, and whether they use text or varchar. Consistency with the codebase beats your personal preference every time — and reviewers will say so.
Verify
npm run db:migrate:tenants
npm run ci:backend

# Then confirm the table is really there, in the right schema:
psql "$DATABASE_URL" -c "\d smartls.onboarding_task"
Justify three decisions20 min

Write down: (1) which ON DELETE you chose for client_id and what happens to tasks when a client is deleted; (2) whether status is a check constraint or a lookup table, and why; (3) which column you indexed and what query you expect it to serve. For each, name the alternative you rejected.

SELF-CHECK 4.4You chose ON DELETE CASCADE for client_id. What have you also decided?
Why: CASCADE is a decision about history, disguised as a housekeeping convenience. In a system with an audit obligation, RESTRICT (forcing an explicit decision) or a soft-delete column is usually right. There is no universally correct answer — the point is that you make the choice knowingly and write it in the migration header.

CHAPTER 5 — BUILD A MODULE  ·  THE BRIEF
46

// Build It Inside Out

Eight files, but not eight equal steps. Build from the pure centre outwards, so that every layer you add sits on something already proven.

#FileWhy hereVerify with
1.rules.jsPure. No dependencies. Testable in milliseconds.A unit test, immediately
2.events.jsThree lines of constants the service will need.It compiles
3.repo.jsSQL against the table you already migrated.A db test
4.service.jsRules + repo + transaction + events + audit.Unit tests with a fake client
5.validator.jsZod schemas including the ai* variants.Parse fixtures directly
6.controller.jsThin. Should be almost mechanical by now.Nothing yet
7.routes.jsThe chain, in the right order.An integration test
8.ai.jsThe manifest over what already exists.The wiring sweep
Why inside-out beats top-down here. If you start at the route, nothing runs until all eight files exist, and your first feedback is an integration test failing for one of six possible reasons. Starting at .rules.js means you have a passing test four minutes in, and every subsequent step adds exactly one new source of failure. That is the same principle as the gates: shrink the distance between a mistake and its detection.
Create the folder
mkdir -p src/modules/operations/onboarding_task
cd src/modules/operations/onboarding_task

# The loader's NAME_RE is /^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*$/ — snake_case only.
# onboardingTask/ would be SILENTLY INVISIBLE. See Chapter 1.
Keep src/modules/sales/lead/ open in a second editor pane for the whole of this chapter. Copying the shape of a known-good module is not cheating — it is the job. What you must not copy is the logic: your lifecycle, fields and rules are your own.
Pick your module key
# Find what is taken. Do not guess.
grep -rho 'MOD-[0-9]\+' src/modules/ | sort -u -t- -k2 -n | tail -20

# Then check the feature catalogue and permission seed data for how a new
# module key is registered — a key that exists only in your routes file
# is a key no role can be granted.
grep -rn "MOD-20" --include=*.js --include=*.sql -l . | head -20
That second command is the real lesson. A module key is not just a string in a routes file — it appears in seed data, the feature catalogue, permission fixtures and tests. Find every place MOD-20 is registered, and register yours in all of them. The feature-catalogue-coverage security test exists precisely because people forget one.
CHAPTER 5 — BUILD A MODULE  ·  THE ORDER OF WORK
47

// Steps 1–3 — The Foundation

Step 1 — onboarding_task.rules.js
  • Export a NEXT map for all four states. Terminal states get [].
  • Export assertTransition(from, to) throwing AppError("BAD_STATE", …, 422).
  • The message must name both states, as lead.rules.js does.
  • No requires other than AppError. If you reach for the db here, stop.
Write it, then test it20 min

Write the file, then write tests/unit/onboarding-task-rules.test.js covering: every legal transition passes; a transition out of a terminal state throws; an unknown from throws; the error's code and status are correct. Run npx jest onboarding-task-rules and paste the output.

Step 2 — onboarding_task.events.js
"use strict";
module.exports = {
  MODULE: "MOD-XX",
  CREATED: "onboarding_task.created",
  UPDATED: "onboarding_task.updated",
  ASSIGNED: "onboarding_task.assigned",
  transition: (status) => "onboarding_task." + String(status).toLowerCase(),
};
Step 3 — onboarding_task.repo.js
  • insert, get, update, list — via the shared helpers, never hand-rolled.
  • update must have the empty-patch guard: no keys ⇒ return the current row.
  • update must pass { touch: "updated_at" }.
  • list must use page(q) for limit/offset and always ORDER BY.
  • Filters: client_id, status, owner_user_id; search q against title.
  • Every user value goes in params, never into the SQL string.
  • One extra query: overdueCount(client) — tasks past due_date and not DONE/CANCELLED.
Watch the overdue query. “Past due” against now() is a timezone question, and due_date is a date, not a timestamptz. Decide explicitly whether a task due today is overdue at 00:01 or at 23:59, and write the decision in a comment. This is exactly the kind of thing that produces a client complaint six months later.
The repo test25 min

Write a db test that inserts three tasks with different statuses and due dates, then asserts: the unfiltered list returns all three in the right order; each filter narrows correctly; a filter with no matches returns [] and not an error; overdueCount matches your stated timezone rule. Paste the passing output.

SELF-CHECK 5.1Your list ignores ?stat=DONE (a typo for status) and returns everything. Is that acceptable?
Why: The shared CRUD kit gained a filterable allow-list for exactly this. A typo that narrows results is a visible bug someone reports; a typo that widens them looks like success. Always fail loudly in the direction of exposing more data than intended.
CHAPTER 5 — BUILD A MODULE  ·  STEPS 1–3 — RULES, EVENTS, REPO
48

// Step 4 — onboarding_task.service.js

The biggest file, and the one that will be reviewed hardest. Five exported functions, each following the anatomy from Chapter 3.

create(client, { data, actor })
  • Wrap the whole body in atomically(client, …).
  • Set status: "PENDING" explicitly — visible in code, not hidden in a column default.
  • owner_user_id: data.owner_user_id || null. Do not fall back to the actor: an unassigned task is a real state the team looks for.
  • emitEvent then audit, both with entityRef from a ref() helper.
  • Return the row.
Note where this deliberately differs from lead. A lead defaults its owner to whoever created it, because an unowned lead is a lead nobody is chasing. An onboarding task defaults to unassigned, because “who still needs an owner?” is the question the team asks every morning. Same shape, opposite default, and the difference is domain knowledge, not code style. Write that reasoning in a comment.
update(client, { id, patch, actor })
  • Read before from the repo. 404 if absent.
  • Refuse edits to DONE or CANCELLED with AppError("LOCKED", …, 422).
  • Copy only allow-listed keys out of patch via a TASK_FIELDS array — the second line of defence behind Zod.
  • audit with both before and after.
transition(client, { id, to, actor })
  • Read before; 404 if absent.
  • assertTransition(before.status, to) — against the row's state, never the client's claim.
  • Update, then emitEvent(events.transition(to)), then audit.
assign(client, { id, ownerUserId, actor })
  • null is a legal value — unassigning is a real operation, not an error.
  • Refuse on terminal states, same as update.
  • Emit ASSIGNED. Audit before and after.
  • Question to answer in a comment: should assigning a PENDING task auto-advance it to IN_PROGRESS? Decide, and justify.
That last question has no right answer, and that is the point. Auto-advancing is convenient and surprising; not auto-advancing is predictable and adds a click. Either is defensible. What is not defensible is choosing without noticing you chose. Your reviewer will ask, and “I hadn't thought about it” is the only wrong reply.
Service tests40 min

Write unit tests with a fake client covering: create emits both an event and an audit row; update on a DONE task throws LOCKED with 422; transition validates against the stored status, not the payload; assign accepts null. Then write down which boundary each test mocks, and what a bug hiding behind that mock would look like in production.

CHAPTER 5 — BUILD A MODULE  ·  STEP 4 — THE SERVICE
49

// Steps 5–8 — Validator, Controller, Routes, AI

Step 5 — onboarding_task.validator.js
  • create: client_id uuid required; title min 1; owner_user_id uuid optional nullable; due_date a date; notes optional.
  • update: written out separately — not create.partial(). Remember API F-17.
  • transition: { to: z.enum([...]) }. assign: { owner_user_id: z.string().uuid().nullable() }.
  • aiTransition and aiAssign: the same, plus task_id: z.string().uuid().
  • The mw(k) factory, verbatim in spirit: safeParse, 422, fieldErrors, req.body = p.data.
  • Export schemas as well as the middlewares. The AI file needs them.
Step 6 — onboarding_task.controller.js
  • One asyncHandler per endpoint. Every one wrapped, no exceptions.
  • const actor = (req) => req.user || { user_id: null };
  • req.tenantDb((c) => service.…) — and never Promise.all over it (PERF-S2).
  • 404 lives here, not in the service. 201 on create.
  • Everything wrapped as { data: … }.
Step 7 — onboarding_task.routes.js
  • router.use(authMiddleware) at the top.
  • MODULE and TRANSITION_ACTION as constants.
  • PATCH: permission → validator → requireLifecyclePermissionOnPatch → controller.
  • POST /:id/transition: validator first, then requireTransitionPermission.
  • module.exports = { basePath: "/onboarding-tasks", feature: …, router }.
The feature key is a real decision. lead exports feature: null, meaning always mounted. If your module should be gated behind a plan or feature flag, name it here and register it in the feature catalogue. Getting this wrong in either direction is a support ticket: a flag nobody can turn on, or a paid feature every plan receives.
Step 8 — onboarding_task.ai.js
  • entity, module_key, screens.
  • reads: list_onboarding_tasks, get_onboarding_task.
  • writes: create_onboarding_task, transition_onboarding_task, assign_onboarding_task.
  • Every write: the same service function, the same Zod schema, the same permission, and confirm: true.
  • describe strings written as prompts — state what the model must supply and what it must not assume.
Write the descriptions last, and carefully20 min

Write all five describe strings. Then reread them as if you were a language model with no other context: could you choose the right tool and fill its arguments from these sentences alone? Rewrite any that fail that test. Compare against convert_lead's, which explicitly warns that a silent fallback is gone.

SELF-CHECK 5.2You give list_onboarding_tasks confirm: true. What have you done?
Why: Confirmation fatigue is a real failure mode. If everything asks, nobody reads the question, and the one dialogue that actually mattered gets the same reflex click. Reads do not confirm; writes always do. The value of a prompt is inversely proportional to how often it appears.

Step 1 — Does it even mount?
npm run dev

# Watch the boot log for your basePath. If it is absent, work down this list:

Point 4 catches almost everyone. A typo in a require path does not crash the server — it makes your module silently not exist, while everything else works perfectly. You will spend twenty minutes testing an endpoint that was never mounted. Read the boot warnings first, every time.

52
