Testing & QA
WEEK 3 · TEACH + BUILD · ~6 HOURS

375 test files in five directories, and they are not five flavours of the same thing. Each answers a different question, and the most interesting category — security/ — does not test behaviour at all. It tests that the codebase still has the shape everyone believes it has.

DirectoryQuestion it answersSpeedMocks?
tests/unit/Does this function do what it says, in isolation?millisecondsHeavily
tests/db/Does this SQL do what I think against a real Postgres?secondsNone
tests/integration/Does the whole request path work end to end?secondsMinimal
tests/security/Is the codebase still shaped the way we assume?fastNone — it reads source
tests/fixtures/Shared setup: not tests, but the reason the others are readable——
The fourth row is what makes this repo unusual. Most codebases test behaviour and hope structure follows. This one asserts structure directly: every route is wired, every mail send point goes through the approved helper, every feature in the catalogue exists, no new silent catch was added. These are the tests that catch the bug nobody wrote a test for, because they test the class of mistake rather than the instance.
The coverage number, and why it is 13
jest.config.js sets exactly one threshold: global: { functions: 13 }. Not lines. Not statements. Not branches. Read the comment above it — it is the best short essay on metrics in the repo.
The finding behind it (TC-Q1)
  • 1The audit measured lines at 40.68% against functions at 13.12%.
  • 2Every *.routes.js reports 100% statements with 0% functions — 99 of them — because requiring the file registers the routes, and that is all the statement counter sees.
  • 3So a gate set on lines or statements would be satisfied by importing files. It would read as healthy while measuring nothing.
  • 4Only 66 of 855 files are at literally 0% statements, which is what makes the codebase look far better instrumented than it is.
And no branches floor, deliberately. “Nobody has measured branch coverage on this repo, and a threshold set to a number someone guessed either fails the build the first time it runs or passes forever without meaning anything. Both outcomes end with the gate being deleted.” That sentence is worth more than most testing books.
SELF-CHECK 6.1Why is 13 described as a ratchet rather than a target?
Why: A target invites gaming: write shallow tests until the number goes green. A ratchet says only “do not make this worse”, which is a claim you can enforce honestly. The comment is explicit that branches should be added and functions raised once CI has printed a real current number — measure first, then set the floor.
CHAPTER 6 — TESTING & QA  ·  375 TESTS, FIVE KINDS
53

// Every Mock Is An Assumption You Stopped Checking

You met this in Chapter 3, in one sentence at the end of the repo comment. It deserves a page, because it is the single most expensive mistake a competent tester makes.

“The conversion failed for every lead, and the unit test did not see it because it mocks clientMaster.create.”
Reconstruct the failure
STEP 1
THE CODE
convert passes client_type (a code) into the client master insert
STEP 2
REALITY
the table has client_type_id, and no client_type column
STEP 3
POSTGRES
42703 — column does not exist. Every conversion, every tenant
STEP 4
THE TEST
mocked clientMaster.create. Green.
The test did not merely fail to catch the bug. It actively certified the broken code as working, and it kept doing so on every CI run while conversions failed in production. A mock does not just remove coverage — it manufactures false confidence, which is strictly worse than no test at all, because no test at least leaves you appropriately nervous.
The rule
Mock what you own and controlYour own pure functions, when you are testing a caller's orchestration rather than the callee's logic.
Mock what is genuinely externalSMTP, an FX rate provider, the LLM API, a payment gateway. Things with cost, latency or side effects outside your system.
Do not mock the databaseIts behaviour — constraints, types, column names, transaction semantics — is precisely the thing most likely to be wrong.
Do not mock across a schema boundaryThe moment a mock stands in for something that reads or writes a table, your test has stopped checking the assumption that matters.
The rule of thumb
If the mock encodes an assumption about a schema, an API contract, or another team's code — write a db or integration test instead. If the mock only avoids slowness or nondeterminism in code you fully control, it is fine.
jest.mock hoisting — a gate of its own
// This LOOKS right and is silently broken:
const service = require("./thing.service");
jest.mock("./thing.repo");        // ← hoisted ABOVE the require by babel-jest…
                                  //   …but reasoning about it here is fragile

// The house rule: jest.mock calls go at the very top, before any require,
// and the CI gate "jest.mock hoisting" enforces it.
  • jest.mock is hoisted by the transform, so its position in the file is misleading about when it takes effect.
  • A mock declared after the module under test has captured a reference can end up mocking nothing.
  • The result is a test that passes for the wrong reason — the worst possible outcome, again.
  • Hence a dedicated CI gate rather than a code-review convention.
Audit your own mocks25 min

Open the service tests you wrote in Chapter 5. For each jest.mock, write: what assumption it encodes, and one concrete production bug that would slip past it. Then convert at least one of them into a db or integration test that would catch that bug. Paste the new test.

CHAPTER 6 — TESTING & QA  ·  WHAT A MOCK COSTS
54

// tests/security/ — Testing The Shape

These files do not start a server or open a database. They read the source tree and assert facts about it. They are the immune system of a codebase that 131 modules and many hands are constantly reshaping.

TestThe drift it prevents
orphan-wiring-sweepA module that exists on disk but is not reachable — because the loader skips a throwing module with a warning, not a crash. Without this test, a broken require is invisible.
feature-catalogue-coverageA feature declared in the catalogue with no module behind it, or a module gated on a feature nobody registered.
mail-send-point-wiringAny code path sending mail without going through the approved helper — bypassing suppression lists, rate limits and the audit trail.
mail-* visibility testsMail templates and recipients drifting out of alignment with what the UI claims will be sent.
no-refresh-auditsAudit rows written for token refreshes, which would bury real security events under routine noise.
signature-*The shape of a critical function changing without its callers being updated.
Six shapes of “declared, not called”
This repo has a name for the recurring family of bugs these tests hunt: a thing is declared, looks present in every review, appears in every doc — and is never actually called. A middleware registered but not mounted. A validator exported but not referenced in the route chain. A handler in the queue map with no producer. A feature in the catalogue with no module. An AI action in the manifest with no catalogue row. A gate in the script list that always exits 0.
“A warning is not a gate.” Repeat it. The module loader warns on a failed module. The lint config permits 136 warnings. A migration can print advice. None of those stop anything. If a condition must not reach production, something has to exit non-zero — and someone has to have checked that it can.
The mail-api-encoding story
  • A payload was being stringified twice before it went out.
  • The API was dead. Every call failed at the far end.
  • The tests were green, because the test asserted on the value before the second stringify.
  • The lesson is the same as the mock lesson, arriving from a different direction: a test that checks an intermediate value proves nothing about what left the building.
Write one
Your own anti-drift test40 min

Write tests/security/onboarding-task-wiring.test.js asserting, by reading source rather than making requests: (1) the module exports the three required keys; (2) every write in the AI manifest has confirm: true; (3) every AI action references a schema that actually exists on the validator; (4) every state in NEXT appears in TRANSITION_ACTION or is deliberately absent to inherit the fail-closed default.

Assertion (4) is the interesting one. It is not obvious whether the right assertion is “every state is listed” or “absence is allowed because the default is safe”. Argue it either way, but pick one and encode it — because an untested convention is not a convention, it is a hope.
CHAPTER 6 — TESTING & QA  ·  THE ANTI-DRIFT TESTS
55

// “No New Silent Catches”

One of the 33 gates, and the clearest example in the repo of how to fix a systemic problem in a live codebase without stopping the world.

The rule
Every catch block whose body is empty or comment-only must carry a marker — @silent:storage, @silent:parse or @silent:teardown — in a block comment inside the catch body, identifying which class from doc/ERROR_HANDLING.md sanctions the swallow.
// Sanctioned — the class is named, so a reader knows it was a decision:
try { localStorage.setItem(k, v); } catch { /* @silent:parse -- bad cache entry */ }

// Not sanctioned — the gate fails:
try { await notify(user); } catch (e) { }
Three design choices worth stealing
  • 1It is a scanner, not a parser. The header says so outright. The vast majority of swallow sites are one of two shapes, and a regex handles both. Richer shapes — “logs to a never-checked variable then throws it away” — are explicitly deferred to a later phase. A tool that catches 90% today beats a perfect one that ships never.
  • 2It ships with a baseline. doc/silent-catch-baseline.json grandfathers the existing violations. The gate therefore passes on day one, and fails only on new ones. This is what makes it a ratchet rather than a wall.
  • 3The escape hatch is honest. --update regenerates the baseline. It exists, it is documented, and using it is visible in the diff — so it is a decision someone has to defend in review, not a silent bypass.
The baseline pattern is the most reusable idea in this chapter. You will inherit codebases with thousands of violations of a rule you want to introduce. Fixing them all first is never funded. A baselined ratchet lets you introduce the rule today, stop the bleeding immediately, and pay down the debt opportunistically. The lint --max-warnings 136 is the same pattern. So is functions: 13.
The taxonomy
  • doc/ERROR_HANDLING.md defines classes A–G of silent catch, only three of which are ever sanctioned.
  • @silent:storage — a best-effort write to a store whose failure genuinely does not matter.
  • @silent:parse — malformed input from a cache or an untrusted blob, where the fallback is to ignore it.
  • @silent:teardown — cleanup on a path that is already failing; the original error is the one that matters.
  • Everything else must be handled, logged with context, or rethrown.
SELF-CHECK 6.2You need to swallow an error on a genuinely new path. What is the correct move?
Why: The header is explicit: adding a new silent catch requires either fixing it — the whole programme's point — or adding a marker with the taxonomy class in the same commit. --update is for regenerating the grandfathered set, not for laundering new debt. And “no class fits” is information, not an obstacle.

Your module works when you drive it by hand. That is the weakest possible evidence. Build the four layers of test that let someone else change your code safely.

6.1Unit — the pure core

6.2Unit — the service
  • Create emits an event and an audit row, inside one transaction.
  • Update on a terminal task throws LOCKED / 422.

  • Assign accepts null; assign on a terminal task refuses.

6.3DB — the SQL
  • Every filter narrows correctly; an empty result is [], not an error.
  • Pagination: page 2 does not repeat page 1 — this is what ORDER BY is for.
  • The empty-patch update returns the current row and does not throw.
  • overdueCount matches the timezone rule you documented.
  • Real Postgres. No mocks.
6.4Integration — the request
  • Each endpoint with a valid token returns its documented status.
  • No token → 401. Wrong permission → 403.
  • Invalid body → 422 with fields populated.
  • The transition your map gates as approve is refused for an edit-only role.
  • An unknown id → 404 with the house error envelope.
Then prove it
npx jest onboarding-task            # your tests only, fast loop
npm run test:coverage               # must not drop the functions floor
npm run ci                          # all 33 gates
The QA note30 min

Write the QA note that ships with your PR: (1) what you tested and at which layer; (2) what you deliberately did not test, and why; (3) the riskiest thing about this change; (4) how a reviewer can verify it themselves in under five minutes. Keep it under 200 words — a note nobody reads has no value.

Point (2) is the mark of a senior engineer. Anyone can list what they tested. Stating the gaps — knowingly, with reasons — is what lets a reviewer aim their attention, and it is the difference between a PR that gets rubber-stamped and one that gets genuinely reviewed.

The Front End
WEEK 3 · TEACH + BUILD · ~8 HOURS · FULL-STACK STARTS HERE

React 18 + Vite + TypeScript, shipped as a PWA, white-labelled per tenant. If you have never written React, this is the chapter you were worried about. It will be fine — because this codebase has a paved road, and the road exists because of a failure worth studying first.

Finding F5 — the root cause of everything else
doc/FE_DESIGN_RULES.md told every new engineer that “the default list screen is <ResourceList>” and that “write-capable lists use <CrudResource>”. crud-resource.tsx never existed. resource-list.tsx existed with zero call sites.
STEP 1
THE DOC
pointed at a deleted component and a dead one
STEP 2
SO
every screen hand-rolled its own list + form
STEP 3
RESULT
24 feature areas each paved their own road
STEP 4
AND
that is the cause of most other findings in the audit
Read that chain again, because it is a management lesson as much as a technical one. A single stale sentence in a document produced two dozen divergent implementations, and every downstream inconsistency — five loading idioms, 28 ad-hoc “Loading…” strings, 11 screens with no empty state — traces back to it. A documented path that does not work is worse than no documentation, because it consumes the good faith of everyone who follows it.
What the audit found downstream
FindingThe symptom
F3No agreed page width; every screen chose its own container
F8Pagination reimplemented per screen, or missing where the endpoint pages
F10Five different loading idioms and 28 ad-hoc “Loading…” strings
F1111 screens with no empty state at all — a blank rectangle
F12The client re-implemented validation as ad-hoc booleans, disagreeing with the API
F13No consistent header, <h1> or primary-action placement
The response: build the road, then build the on-ramp
  • 1–4Phases 1–4 built the road — ListPage, Form, the design tokens, and the CI gates that keep them honest.
  • 5Phase 5 built the on-ramp — npm run new:screen. Its header says it exactly: “the thing that makes the paved road the path of least resistance rather than the path you take after reading a document.”
That is the whole philosophy. You do not get consistency by writing rules; you get it by making the correct thing the easiest thing. Every time you are tempted to write a convention document, ask first whether you could write a generator, a gate, or a component instead.
CHAPTER 7 — THE FRONT END  ·  THE PAVED ROAD
59

// <ListPage> — What It Owns

One component, composed once, so that a screen author stops re-deciding six things that have a correct answer.

It owns
  • The page container and its width (F3) — wide, standard, reading, full.
  • The header, its <h1> and its primary action (F13).
  • All four states — loading, error, empty, populated — routed to the right primitive every time (F10, F11).
  • The toolbar slot, so filters sit in the same place on every screen.
  • Pagination, when the endpoint pages (F8).
It deliberately does not own
Data fetching and forms. It takes a useList result rather than a path, “because half the list screens in this app derive their rows — filtering, joining an id→name map, merging two endpoints — and a component that fetched for them would be immediately escaped.” The header goes further: <CrudResource>'s promise of a declarative fields spec “is exactly the abstraction that was documented, never built, and would not have fitted these screens.”
An abstraction that people escape is worse than no abstraction. It costs you the learning curve and the inconsistency, because now you have the framework's way, the escaped way, and an argument about which is correct. Design for the eighty percent and leave a clean exit for the rest.
CHAPTER 7 — THE FRONT END  ·  <ListPage>
60

// A Whole Screen, In One Component

This is a complete, production-shaped list screen. Read it and count what you did not have to decide.

export function ClientsPage() {
  const { rows, error, loading, reload } = useList<Client>("/clients");
  const [q, setQ] = React.useState("");
  const [open, setOpen] = React.useState(false);
  const shown = React.useMemo(
    () => (rows ?? []).filter((r) => r.name.toLowerCase().includes(q.toLowerCase())),
    [rows, q],
  );

  return (
    <ListPage
      title="Clients"
      description="Every party you invoice. Credit limits come from the master record."
      action={<Button onClick={() => setOpen(true)}>New client</Button>}
      toolbar={<Input value={q} onChange={(e) => setQ(e.target.value)}
                      placeholder="Search clients…" className="max-w-xs" />}
      columns={columns}
      rows={shown}
      error={error}
      loading={loading}
      rowKey={(r) => r.client_id}
      empty="No clients yet."
      emptyFiltered="No clients match that search."
    />
  );
}
The two empty states
empty and emptyFiltered are separate props, and both are required. “No clients yet” invites you to create one. “No clients match that search” tells you to clear the filter. Showing the first when the second is true is how a user concludes their data has been deleted. Two words of copy, one support ticket avoided — and making it a required prop is what guarantees the author thinks about it.
SELF-CHECK 7.1Why does ListPage take rows rather than a path to fetch?
Why: The header names the precedent by file: a fetching scaffold was documented, one was built with zero call sites, and both are gone. The component draws its boundary at the point where screens genuinely agree — layout and states — and stops before the point where they genuinely differ.

// Forms — One Schema, Two Sides

The most valuable idea in the front end, and the direct answer to finding F12.

F12 — the client disagreeing with the API
“The client used to re-implement the rules as ad-hoc booleans — e.g. finance/pages.tsx:141's canSubmit.” Two definitions of valid, in two languages, maintained by two people. They diverge on the first change, and the user finds out by having a form accepted and then rejected.
The fix: packages/shared
STEP 1
packages/shared
the Zod schema, written once
STEP 2
API
imports it to validate the request body
STEP 3
CLIENT
imports it via useZodForm
STEP 4
RESULT
they cannot disagree
export function useZodForm<TSchema extends z.ZodType<FieldValues>>(
  schema: TSchema,
  options?: Omit<UseFormProps<z.input<TSchema>>, "resolver">,
) {
  return useForm<z.input<TSchema>>({
    resolver: zodResolver(schema),
    mode: "onTouched",     // ← see below
    ...options,
  });
}
mode: "onTouched", and why not onChange
Straight from the source: it “validates on submit, then re-validates a field as the user leaves it. Not onChange: telling someone their date is malformed while they are still typing it is the single most disliked form behaviour there is.” A one-word config option, a real decision about how it feels to use the software, and a comment so the next person does not innocently ‘improve’ it.
Two CI gates protect this
GateWhat it checks
Shared schema packageThe package builds and its exports resolve from both sides.
Shared-schema gateThe client is not re-implementing validation the shared package already defines — F12 cannot come back quietly.
The form primitives
<Form>The provider; wires the useZodForm instance.
<FormField>Label, input, description and error, in the right order, with the right aria- wiring.
<FormError>Field-level errors, populated from the API's fields object on a 422.
<FormButtons>Submit and cancel, consistently placed, with the disabled-while-submitting behaviour done once.
<Dialog>Writes happen in a dialog over the list, not on a separate route — so context is never lost.
Notice the loop closing. The API returns 422 with fields because lead.validator.js passes p.error.flatten().fieldErrors through. <FormError> exists to render exactly that. The two ends of a design decision made in Chapter 3 finally meet here — this is what “full-stack” actually means: seeing the whole arc of one idea.

When documentation causes an incident, the fix is a gate on the documentation.
A Node-version story worth reading
"//engines": "Mirrors the root package.json and .nvmrc. The client is linted,
 tested and built on Node 20 in CI and in the Docker image, so a dev tree on a
 newer Node can silently accept a dependency that CI cannot run — exactly how
 jsdom@30 (which needs undici@8 / Node >=22.19) got in and broke the frontend
 job. Declaring it here makes npm emit EBADENGINE locally instead."
  • A developer on a newer Node installed a dependency their machine supported.
  • CI runs Node 20. The frontend job broke, for everyone, on a change that looked unrelated.
  • The fix is not a rule about which Node to use — it is engines, so npm refuses locally.
  • Move the failure from CI to the developer's terminal. That is the whole art of this.
SELF-CHECK 7.2Why does the raw-palette gate matter more here than in a typical app?
Why: Multi-tenancy has a front-end dimension people forget. Every hardcoded colour is a place where tenant branding silently fails, and it will be found by the client, not by you. The gate turns a class of bug that is invisible in development into a build failure.
CHAPTER 7 — THE FRONT END  ·  THE FRONTEND GATES
63

// The Outbox, and Why The Server Had To Change

client/src/lib/outbox.ts is the best full-stack story in the codebase: a front-end feature that could not be built until the backend grew a middleware. Read it and you understand why “full-stack” is a way of thinking, not a list of technologies.

Two layers of rescue
lib/form-draft.tsRescues what you typed. The tab closed, the browser crashed — the half-filled form comes back.
lib/outbox.tsRescues what you submitted. You filled the form, pressed Save, and the request never left the machine. Before this: a red banner and a retyped form.
The problem that makes naive replay dangerous
“A rejected fetch does NOT mean the request never arrived.” It means no response came back — and “the request died on the way out” and “the request was processed and the response died on the way back” are indistinguishable from the browser. Replaying blindly risks posting a journal entry, an invoice or a payment twice. In an OHADA ledger that is not a rough edge, it is a material misstatement — and it would be a strictly worse bug than the one this feature set out to fix.
The fix spans both sides
STEP 1
CLIENT
generate an Idempotency-Key once, at first attempt
STEP 2
REPLAY
reuse the same key on every retry
STEP 3
SERVER
middleware/idempotency.js + migration 0662 store the outcome
STEP 4
RESULT
a replay of completed work returns the original response
Recall from Chapter 1 exactly where that middleware sits: above the module loader, so it covers all ~700 tenant writes without any module opting in; and below tenantContext, because it needs req.tenantDb. Position in a middleware chain is an architectural decision, and this is what it buys.
Two more rules from the same file
  • 1Order is preserved. Entries replay oldest-first, one at a time.
  • 2Failures stop the line. A network failure mid-flush leaves the rest queued. “An ERP write sequence is frequently causal — create the dossier, then cost it, then invoice it — and replaying the third after the first has failed produces a 404 storm and a queue full of ‘rejected’ entries that were never wrong.”
And the counterfactual, stated plainly in the source: without server-side idempotency, “this file would have to ask the user to confirm every queued write — which, at that point, is just the retyping we were avoiding.” The feature would have existed, shipped, and delivered nothing. Knowing when a front-end feature is impossible without a backend change is the single most valuable thing a full-stack engineer contributes.

08
Jobs, Queues & Events
WEEK 3 · TEACH + LAB · ~5 HOURS

Rendering a PDF, sending an email, syncing FX rates, sweeping overdue records — none of these belong inside a request. This chapter covers the second runtime: a separate container, BullMQ over Redis, and 44 handlers. It also contains the two best failure stories in the entire codebase.

Two processes, one image
APIWorker
Commandnode src/server.jsnode src/jobs/workers.js
Docker stageruntimeworker
ConsumesHTTP requestsBullMQ queues on Redis
Has req?YesNo — and this is the source of most job bugs
ScalingHorizontal, behind the proxyHorizontal — which is why cron needs a lock
The producer side
async function enqueue(name, jobName, data, opts = {}) {
  return getProducer(name).add(jobName, data, {
    removeOnComplete: 1000,
    removeOnFail: 5000,
    attempts: 3,
    backoff: { type: "exponential", delay: 5000 },
    ...opts,
  });
}
  • attempts: 3Three tries, then the job is failed. Which means every handler must be idempotent — attempt 2 may follow a partial attempt 1.
  • backoffExponential from 5s. A downstream service that is down stays down for a few seconds; hammering it immediately makes recovery slower.
  • removeOnFail: 5000Failures are kept five times longer than successes. Successes are noise; failures are the evidence you need at 2am.
  • Lazy producersQueues are created on first use and cached, sharing the app's Redis connection. No connection storm at boot.
attempts: 3 is a contract with every handler you will ever write. If your job sends an email and then updates a row, and it crashes between the two, attempt 2 sends a second email. Retries are not free reliability — they are a requirement placed on your code. Design the handler so that running it twice is indistinguishable from running it once.
CHAPTER 8 — JOBS, QUEUES & EVENTS  ·  WORK THAT OUTLIVES THE REQUEST
67

// NEW-04: A Perfect Design That Never Ran

Open src/jobs/corn-lock.js. Note the filename — we will come back to it. Read the comment at line 30. It is the most important thing in this chapter.

What the module is for
node-cron fires wherever a worker process runs. With two worker instances — or ENABLE_WORKERS=true on the API next to a dedicated worker — every cron would run twice: double email sends, double reminders, double billing. withCronLock(name, fn) makes each named job single-flight across all processes sharing the database.
And the design is genuinely good
  • pg_try_advisory_lock(hashtext(key)) — non-blocking, so a losing instance skips rather than queueing up a second run for later.
  • Session-scoped, not transaction-scoped, so fn is not wrapped in a long-lived transaction and jobs open their own transactions freely on other connections.
  • Crash-safe: if the process dies mid-job, the connection drops and Postgres releases the lock automatically.
  • If the unlock fails on a broken connection, the client is destroyed rather than returned to the pool, so a stale lock can never ride a recycled connection.
Now the comment
“This used to import config/database, whose initDatabase() IS NEVER CALLED ANYWHERE IN src/ — proven: getPool() throws ‘db pool not initialised’. So EVERY cron job wrapped in withCronLock threw on its first line, and because jobs swallow their own errors that failure was invisible. The module read as working code with a sensible advisory-lock design and had never once acquired a lock.”
Sit with that. Every element was right: the algorithm, the crash-safety, the pool hygiene, the documentation. It imported the wrong module. It threw on its first line, on every tick, since the day it was written — and the error was swallowed by the very jobs it was protecting. Nobody was wrong, and nothing worked.
Three lessons, and they compound
  • 1Silent catches turn a crash into a lie. The jobs swallowed their own errors, so a total failure looked identical to a successful no-op. This is why “no new silent catches” is one of the 33 gates.
  • 2Dead initialisation is invisible. initDatabase() existed, looked essential, and was called by nothing. This is the “declared, not called” family again — the sixth shape.
  • 3Code review cannot catch this. Every line is correct in isolation; the defect is in a relationship between files. Only running it — or a test that asserts the lock is actually acquired — finds it.
And the filename
src/jobs/corn-lock.js    # the real implementation — note the typo
src/jobs/cron-lock.js    # "Alias for corn-lock.js so both imports resolve."
Someone typed corn. Rather than a rename that would break unknown importers, an alias module was added so both spellings resolve. Pragmatic, honest, and documented. It is also a small ongoing tax, and a reminder that a typo in a filename outlives everyone's memory of it. When you notice one on day one, say so — that is the cheapest moment it will ever be.
SELF-CHECK 8.1What test would have caught NEW-04 on the day it shipped?
Why: A mocked pool is precisely how the bug survives — the mock supplies the pool the real code could not get. The assertion has to be behavioural and against reality: did fn run, was the lock genuinely acquired, and does a second concurrent caller skip? This is the mock lesson from Chapter 6 in its most expensive form.
CHAPTER 8 — JOBS, QUEUES & EVENTS  ·  THE LOCK THAT NEVER LOCKED
68

// workers.js — And The 0-Byte Stub

The second story. The producer side worked perfectly. Any process could enqueue a durable job. It was reliable, retried, and backed off politely.

“It was a 0-byte stub — any job enqueued would have sat in Redis forever with nothing to process it.”
Half a system is not half as useful; it is zero useful, and it looks fine. The enqueue call returns a job id. No error surfaces anywhere. The queue depth climbs in a Redis nobody is watching. This is the same shape as NEW-04 and the same shape as the mail double-stringify: the failure is silent because the missing half is the half that would have complained.
The registry today
const PROCESSORS = [
  { name: "regie-aging",              concurrency: 1, handler: require("./handlers/regie-aging") },
  { name: "regie-aging-scheduler",    concurrency: 1, handler: require("./handlers/regie-aging-scheduler") },
  { name: "pdf",                      concurrency: 2, handler: require("./handlers/pdf-render") },
  { name: "email",                    concurrency: 3, handler: require("./handlers/email-send") },
  { name: "fx-sync",                  concurrency: 1, handler: require("./handlers/fx-sync") },
  { name: "fx-sync-scheduler",        concurrency: 1, handler: require("./handlers/fx-sync-scheduler") },
  { name: "ai-transcribe",            concurrency: 2, handler: require("./handlers/ai-transcribe") },
  { name: "scheduled-report",         concurrency: 1, handler: require("./handlers/scheduled-report") },
  { name: "scheduled-report-scheduler", concurrency: 1, handler: require("./handlers/scheduled-report-scheduler") },
  /* … 44 handler files in total … */
];
Read the pairing
  • fx-sync and fx-sync-scheduler. regie-aging and regie-aging-scheduler. scheduled-report and scheduled-report-scheduler.
  • A worker without a scheduler is a job nobody starts. The comment on scheduled-report-scheduler says it outright: the worker “was registered from the day reports shipped and enqueued by nothing — its own header deferred the trigger to ‘an app scheduled-task or external cron’, which was never part of the repo, so a scheduled report only ran if somebody POSTed the route.”
  • When you add a background job, ask immediately: what enqueues this? If the answer is a document, the answer is nothing.
And a worker for a surface that did not exist
ai-vision “was registered here and enqueued by nothing. It fed a document-scan turn to the assistant — but the assistant has no image entry point: no route, no validator, no upload control, nothing. It was a worker for a surface that was never built, and the general orphan sweep is what finally said so.” Note how it was removed: the capability lives on in services/ai/vision.service with three real callers, and the comment records that restoring the chat flow means building its route first, “at which point this handler is a git show away.”
That is how to delete code. Not silently, and not never. Remove it, and leave a comment saying what it did, why it went, what still works, and how to bring it back. The git history is searchable only by someone who already suspects the thing existed.
Concurrency is a decision
  • 1pdf: 2 — Puppeteer is memory-hungry; two renders is what the container can hold.
  • 3email: 3 — SMTP throughput, balanced against the sending domain's reputation.
  • 1fx-sync: 1 — a single upstream provider with rate limits; parallelism would only earn 429s.
  • 1The signing-reminder pair, both at 1: “the sweep sends outbound email and the cap is enforced in SQL, so parallelism would buy nothing and risk a burst against the sending domain.”

69

// emit.js — Two Logs, One Transaction

Every service you write calls these two functions. They look similar and are not.

emitEvent → live.event_logDrives behaviour: notifications, workflows, compliance triggers. Something is expected to react.
audit → live.immutable_ledgerAppend-only trail, 10-year retention. Nothing reacts; it is the permanent record of who did what.
The error policy, precisely
“Both are best-effort-safe: a logging failure must not break the business op, EXCEPT audit of security-critical actions which should bubble up.” A failed notification should not roll back an invoice. A failed audit of a permission change should — because an unlogged privilege escalation is exactly the event the log exists for.
Watch-the-Watcher
Implemented here, centrally, “so every security-critical event is caught no matter which module emits it — rather than wiring a notifier into each of the three (permission/role/field_visibility) services separately and missing the next one someone adds.”
How it works
  • 1event_type.is_security_critical, seeded in 9020_seed_rbac_events.sql, is the single source of truth.
  • 2For those events the event_log row's priority is forced to HIGH.
  • 3A HIGH in-app notification is fanned out to every active CEO and MANAGEMENT user — the watchers.
  • 4Both run in the caller's transaction, so the notification is atomic with the change that triggered it. There is no window in which the privilege exists and the alert does not.
  • 5The fan-out is a single INSERT…SELECT guarded by an EXISTS, so it is a zero-row no-op for the ~99% of events that are NORMAL — no branching round-trip in JS.
Point 5 is a craft detail worth stealing. The obvious implementation is if (isSecurityCritical) { await notify(); } — which costs a round-trip to find out on every single event in the system. Pushing the condition into the SQL makes the common case free. Correctness first, then make the common path cost nothing.
Correlation ids without threading a parameter
function currentRequestId() {
  const ctx = requestContext.get();     // AsyncLocalStorage
  return (ctx && ctx.requestId) || null;
}
“Read from AsyncLocalStorage rather than threaded through every caller: there are hundreds of emit/audit sites, and a parameter that 300 call sites have to remember to pass is a parameter that will be missing somewhere.” It returns null when there is no request — a BullMQ worker, a scheduler, a migration. That null is information, not a gap.
SELF-CHECK 8.2Why must the Watch-the-Watcher notification run inside the caller's transaction?
Why: Atomicity is the feature. Any design where the change and the alert can diverge has a window an attacker can aim at — and even without an attacker, an intermittent notification failure quietly destroys trust in the whole alerting system.
CHAPTER 8 — JOBS, QUEUES & EVENTS  ·  EVENTS, AUDIT & THE WATCHER
70

// Two Rules That Decide Everything

doc/ERROR_HANDLING.md opens with two sentences, and the entire seven-class taxonomy is derived from them. Learn the two rules and you can classify any failure you meet.

1. A mutation is never silent. If server state changed — or was meant to — the user is told.
2. “Don't interrupt the user” and “don't tell engineering” are different decisions. Conflating them is what .catch(() => {}) does, “and why a background sync could fail for every user for a week with no signal at all.”
Rule 2 is the one nobody thinks of. A single catch that does nothing is making two decisions at once: do not bother the user, and do not tell the team. Those have completely different correct answers for background work. Separating them is the whole design.
The seven classes
ClassWhenToast?Report?
A · StoragelocalStorage fails on quota or private modenonenone
B · Parse fallbackMalformed cache entry or body, with a defined fallbacknonenone
C · TeardownClosing something already gone; the original error is the useful onenonenone
D · Best-effort backgroundFire-and-forget the user did not initiate — read receipts, telemetrynonenotice
E · Degraded readPartial UI is acceptable, but the user must see the degradationinline notenotice
F · MutationAnything that changes server statealwayswarning+
G · ConfigA prerequisite is unset — SMTP, an API key, a geofence policycallout + fix-it linknever
  • A, B and C carry the @silent:* markers the CI gate checks. D is where the old code was wrong: silent to the user, but it must still reach engineering.
  • G never reports. A missing API key is not an engineering incident, it is a configuration task — and paging the team for it trains them to ignore the channel.
  • F is never silent, full stop. There is no marker that sanctions it.
CHAPTER 8 — JOBS, QUEUES & EVENTS  ·  THE ERROR CONTRACT
71

// The Mutation Envelope

Rule 1 said a mutation is never silent. This is the shape that makes it true.

{ "ok": true, "changed": true,  "data": { … } }
{ "ok": true, "changed": false, "message": "Session was already revoked" }
  • 1ok:false is never returned. Failures throw and are handled by middleware/error-handler.js. One path for errors, not two.
  • 2changed answers “did server state actually move?” This is the case that made the session-kill bug look like nothing happened: a second click to revoke an already-revoked session succeeds with a 200 whose body says the row was unchanged.
  • 3The client renders that as “That session was already revoked”, not silence. The user's mental model stays correct.
Why changed:false is not a 409. An already-revoked session is not a conflict. “Making idempotent success a 4xx would break the offline outbox — it replays writes that failed offline, and a replayed successful kill would then surface as an error for an operation that worked.” Genuine conflicts — a stale-record edit, a double-post — keep 409; idempotent no-ops keep 200 with changed:false.
Chapter 7's outbox and this status-code decision are the same decision, seen from two ends. You cannot choose 409 here without breaking a front-end feature three layers away. This is exactly the reasoning that a full-stack engineer can do and two specialists, each correct in their own domain, cannot.
The rollout, and the honest default
  • withResult() in src/shared/crud/ was applied to ~25 action endpoints — /kill, /revoke-all, /approve, /transition, /post, /purge, /supersede, /regularize.
  • useAction treats a missing envelope as changed:true, so the ~466 routes not yet converted still work.
  • A later PR converts the rest and flips the default.
  • The baseline pattern again: introduce the contract today, keep the old world working, migrate incrementally, flip the default last.
SELF-CHECK 8.3Your new /onboarding-tasks/:id/assign is called with the owner it already has. What should it return?
Why: It is an idempotent no-op, not a conflict, and the client should say so out loud rather than flashing a success that implies work happened. Answer 4 is the subtle trap: it is technically a success, but it lies about whether state moved — and an outbox replay would then look like a real second assignment.

# Run a second worker to prove the lock

Defend it in writing20 min

Write the paragraph you would put in the PR: exactly why running this handler twice produces the same result as running it once. Name the mechanism — a uniqueness constraint, a state check, a marker column, a dedupe key. If your answer is “it probably won't run twice”, you have not answered.

“It probably won't run twice” is the sentence that precedes every duplicate-billing incident. Retries, redeploys mid-job, a network partition that makes a completed job look failed, an operator re-running something manually — all of these happen, and none of them are exotic. Write the mechanism down, and if there isn't one, build one.

LLM Integration
WEEK 3 · TEACH + BUILD · ~6 HOURS

An assistant that can read and write real ERP records on behalf of a real user. Every safety property in this design was earned — one of them by a High-severity audit finding that is the best security lesson in the codebase. Read the loop first, then the finding.

The loop, from the source header
STEP 1
RECALL
retrieve context; redact before egress
STEP 2
PLAN
function-calling against the tool list
STEP 3
GATE
Zod-validate proposed actions (≤2 self-correct)
STEP 4
CONFIRM
return action cards for a human to approve
STEP 5
EXECUTE
run with the user's permissions
STEP 6
LOG
immutable ledger, every time
“The AI never exceeds the calling user; sensitive text is redacted before egress.” Those two clauses are the entire security posture, and the rest of this chapter is how each is actually enforced — because for a while, one of them was not.
Three numbers that control cost
ConstantValueThe trade-off it encodes
HISTORY_TURNS20Stored history is unbounded; this caps only what is re-sent, so cost per call stays flat however long the thread grows. ~10 exchanges.
SUMMARY_BATCH10How many messages fall out of the window before the summary regenerates.
NARRATION_TURNS5Confirmation narration needs “what was just done and the step before” — not 20 turns of context on every confirm.
And the honesty about what that costs
On SUMMARY_BATCH: “Regenerating on every turn would mean a second model call per question — roughly doubling the cost of a long thread, against a budget that is hard-capped per tenant. Batching makes it one extra call per ten turns. The price is a gap: up to SUMMARY_BATCH - 1 messages can sit outside both the replay window and the summary, so a detail mentioned exactly there is briefly unavailable until the next batch absorbs it. Bounded, self-correcting, and much cheaper than the alternative — but real, so it is written down rather than discovered.”
“Written down rather than discovered.” That is the standard. Every engineering decision has a downside; the difference between a good codebase and a bad one is whether the downside is documented at the point of the trade-off or found by a user eighteen months later. When you make a trade-off, name the cost in a comment.

74

// SEC H1: Recording Is Not Preventing

Open src/services/ai/action-authz.js and read its header. This is the most instructive security finding in the repository, and it is worth reading twice.

The setup — everything looked right
  • 1The AI action catalogue has carried a required_permission column from the start.
  • 2The registrar populates it from each module's manifest.
  • 3The orchestrator even SELECTs it into the tool list.
  • 4IT WAS NEVER COMPARED AGAINST ANYTHING.
// Both execution sites, verbatim:
const out    = fn ? await fn({ client, user, payload }) : { error: "no executor" };
const result = await fn({ client, user, payload });
Why it survived review
“Authorization in this codebase lives exclusively in route middleware — services do not check grants. action-registry.js says of its executors: each calls a module SERVICE with the caller's client + identity (module RBAC/audit applies). The audit half was true. The RBAC half was not — and the assistant router carries only authMiddleware plus a tenant-wide feature flag.”
So the assistant was a general-purpose bypass around the module grant matrix, available to every authenticated user in any tenant with AI enabled.
What that meant in practice
  • Ten write actions were reachable that way: create_client, open_dossier, update_dossier, transition_dossier, create_costing, draft_quotation, draft_final_invoice, draft_purchase_order, draft_supplier_invoice, draft_cash_request.
  • “A warehouse operator holding only WMS grants could ask the assistant, in ordinary language, to draft a supplier invoice and a cash request — creating financial documents they cannot create through any screen or route available to them.”
  • “Every one was faithfully written to the immutable ledger, so the audit trail would have recorded the unauthorized action accurately.”
“Recording is not preventing.” Four words worth engraving. The audit trail worked flawlessly. It would have given you a perfect, timestamped, attributable record of every unauthorised financial document — after the fact. Observability and control are different systems solving different problems, and a beautiful audit log can make a team feel safe while nothing is actually stopping anything.
The root cause, generalised
Remember the “declared, not called” family from Chapter 6? This is its most dangerous member. The column existed. It was populated. It was read into memory. The comparison was never written. Every artefact of the security control was present except the one line that enforces it — and every reviewer who checked “is there a permission column?” got a yes.
SELF-CHECK 9.1What kind of test catches SEC H1?
Why: The test has to be adversarial and end-to-end: a real low-privilege identity attempting a real out-of-scope action. Every narrower test passes on the broken code — the column is there, the registrar fills it, the orchestrator reads it. Test the property you care about (“this user cannot do that”), not the mechanism you built to provide it.
CHAPTER 9 — LLM INTEGRATION  ·  SEC H1 — THE BYPASS
75

// The Fix, And Its Uncomfortable Rule

action-authz.js now compares the action's required_permission against the caller's grants. But the interesting part is what it does when there is no requirement to compare.

“An action whose required_permission is null does not execute.”
“That is the opposite of the usual instinct — ‘no requirement means no restriction’ — and it is deliberate: a missing requirement means the catalogue is incomplete, and the safe reading of an incomplete authorization record is no. A registrar that forgets to declare a permission produces a visibly broken action rather than an invisibly open one.”
Visibly broken beats invisibly open
Invisibly openThe action works. Everyone is happy. Nobody knows the permission is missing. It is found by an auditor, or by an incident.
Visibly brokenThe action fails on first use. Someone files a bug within the hour. The fix is one line in a manifest.
Write that comparison on a card and keep it. Given a choice between a failure mode users will report immediately and one nobody will notice, choose the loud one — even when it costs you a support ticket. The quiet failure is not cheaper; its bill just arrives later, with interest.
You have now seen fail-closed three times
WhereThe unlisted / missing case
lead.routes.jsA transition not in TRANSITION_ACTION defaults to approve — the higher permission.
query-helpers.jsAn identifier not matching IDENT_RE is rejected, not sanitised and passed.
action-authz.jsAn action with no declared permission does not run.
Three unrelated subsystems, one principle, applied consistently. That consistency is what makes a codebase learnable: once you know how this team resolves ambiguity, you can predict the behaviour of code you have not read. Apply it in your own module and reviewers will recognise it immediately.
Reads are gated too
  • The header is explicit that reads are gated, not just writes.
  • A read action returns tenant data the caller may not be entitled to see — a list of financial documents is a disclosure even if nothing is written.
  • The Chapter 3 principle again: hidden money is null, not zero. Here, an ungranted read is refused, not silently emptied.

// llm.service.js — Vendor-Agnostic By Construction

Three practical lessons about integrating a model provider, all of which apply to any third-party API you will ever wire up.

1. DB-first, env-fallback, then degrade
const PRIMARY  = "deepseek";
const FALLBACK = "gemini";

async function resolveVendor(client, name) {
  const db = await platformVendors.getConfig(name);
  if (db && db.is_active !== false && db.api_key && db.endpoint_url) return db;
  const env = ENV_VENDORS[name];
  if (env && env.api_key && env.endpoint_url) return env;
  return null;
}
  • 1Platform database first — one shared, encrypted platform.ai_vendor_credential set, rotatable without a deploy.
  • 2.env fallback — BUILD_CONVENTIONS §7, so local development works with no platform record.
  • 3If neither is set, the call degrades to a clear stub. Not a crash, not a hang, not a silent empty answer — a stub that says what is missing.
Point 3 is class G from the error taxonomy. An unconfigured API key is not an incident, it is a configuration task — so it produces a callout with a fix-it link, and it never pages engineering. Notice how the taxonomy you learned in Chapter 8 predicts the correct behaviour here without anyone having to think about it again.
2. All vendors speak one shape
  • Every configured vendor exposes an OpenAI-compatible /chat/completions endpoint.
  • The adapter layer is therefore thin, and adding a vendor is a database row, not a code change.
  • Standardising on the widest-supported wire format is how you stay vendor-agnostic in practice, as opposed to in an architecture diagram.
3. The markup-leak defence — models misbehave
// Some models (notably DeepSeek, esp. when handed a large tool list) emit their
// tool-call markup as TEXT in `content` instead of the structured `tool_calls`
// field. Left as-is it leaks raw markup to the user and the real action never runs.
const TOOLCALL_MARKUP = /[｜▁]|DSML|invoke\s+name="/i;
  • ATwo failures in one bug: the user sees raw markup, and the action silently never runs.
  • BThe recovery parses out any usable calls and, either way, strips the markup so the user never sees it. Fix the visible symptom and the invisible one.
  • CThe pattern is anchored on the actual markup characters — the full-width pipe, the ▁ token, the literal DSML marker, an invoke name=" tag — “so it never false-triggers on prose that merely says tool calls.”
Lesson C is the one people skip. A defensive regex that fires on ordinary text is a new bug wearing the costume of a fix — and a user asking “how do tool calls work?” getting their sentence mangled is a genuinely baffling support ticket. Anchor on structure, never on vocabulary.
Redaction before egress
  • redact.js covers IBAN, card numbers with separators, OHADA-zone RIB bank accounts, Cameroon NIU tax IDs, social security numbers, phones and emails.
  • “For a system handling OHADA financial data, these are not edge cases.” The original three patterns missed most of them.
  • Pattern-based, not NER-based, and the reason is stated: NER for person names “would require a model call or a library dependency this layer cannot afford on every egress path”.
  • “ORDER MATTERS: more specific patterns must run before general ones. A RIB with spaces would be partially caught by the phone pattern if it ran first.”
Localisation is a security requirement, not a nicety. A redaction library built for US and EU formats would pass every test written by its authors and leak Cameroonian tax IDs on day one. Know the data your clients actually hold.

Treating prompts as code — testable, improvable, owned — is the difference between an AI feature that works and one that works on the demo.

G3
Gate 3 — End of Week Three
PROVE IT · BEFORE WEEK 4 OPENS · SIGNED OFF BY YOUR LEAD

Three weeks in, and your feature now exists at every layer: a screen, an API, a service, SQL, a background job and an AI action. This gate asks whether it is one coherent thing or six things that happen to share a name.

G3.1Front end
  • My screen is on the paved road, scaffolded through the generator.
  • Both empty states exist, and their copy differs.
  • Zero client-side validation of my own — the shared schema is the only source of truth.
  • All eleven frontend gates are green.
  • I can explain F5 and why the “frontend guide is not lying” gate exists.
  • I have seen my own write queue and replay while offline.
G3.2Jobs and errors
  • Handler and scheduler both shipped; single-fire proven with two workers running.
  • I can state my handler's idempotency mechanism — not a hope that it will not run twice.
  • I can classify any failure into the seven-class taxonomy and say what it should show the user.
  • I can explain changed:false, and why making it a 409 would break the outbox.
  • I can tell the NEW-04 story and say what test would have caught it.
G3.3AI
  • My AI action reuses the same service, schema and permission as the HTTP route.
  • The ungranted user is refused, and I have the integration test that proves it.
  • I can tell the SEC H1 story and explain “recording is not preventing”.
  • I can explain why a null required_permission refuses to execute.
  • I tuned my describe strings against five real phrasings and recorded the before and after.

You have now followed a single idea — a task that someone in an office needs to tick off — from a React dialog through a shared Zod schema, an Express chain, a service, a transaction, SQL, an event, a queue, and a language model, and back. Week 4 is about getting it to a client and keeping it there.

Notifications, Email & Push
WEEK 3 · TEACH + LAB · ~5 HOURS · THE OUTBOUND EDGE

Everything you have built so far happens while someone is looking at the screen. This chapter is about the opposite case: the invoice was approved at 23:40, the person who needs to know is asleep, and the system has to reach them. Three channels, one producer, and a set of rules about which of them a user is allowed to switch off.

One producer, three channels
Every notification in this system goes through one function: notify() in src/modules/notification/notification.service.js, with a bulk sibling notifyMany(). Nothing in the codebase sends a user-facing alert any other way. That single door is what makes preferences, categories, dedupe and security rules enforceable at all — a second door would be a second place to forget them.
ChannelStorageOpt-in modelFailure behaviour
IN_APPTenant notification table — the source of truthDefault ONPart of the caller's transaction. If this fails, the business write fails.
EMAILSMTP via email.serviceDefault OFF — explicitly opt-inBest effort. Logged, never thrown.
PUSHWeb-Push / VAPID to registered devicesSubscribing is the opt-inBest effort. Logged, never thrown.
Read the defaults column again, because it encodes a judgement. In-app is on by default because it costs the user nothing — it waits in a list until they look. Email is off by default because it arrives in a place they did not choose to open, and a system that emails by default trains people to filter it. Push has no default at all: the act of granting permission and subscribing a device is consent, so there is nothing separate to switch on.
The one thing a user cannot switch off
Categories are declared in src/shared/notifications/categories.js, and exactly one of them carries security: true.
const CATEGORIES = [
  { key: "security",   label: "Security",     security: true  },
  { key: "approvals",  label: "Approvals",    security: false },
  { key: "finance",    label: "Finance",      security: false },
  { key: "operations", label: "Operations",   security: false },
  { key: "sales",      label: "Sales & CRM",  security: false },
  { key: "compliance", label: "Compliance",   security: false },
  { key: "system",     label: "System",       security: false },
];
  • Security notifications ignore every preference, on every channel. The service comment states the rule in one line: a user cannot silence “your password changed”.
  • That is not paternalism. The whole value of a breach alert is that the attacker — who may now be holding the account — cannot turn it off.
  • Everything else is tunable per (channel, category), which is the grain a human actually thinks in. Nobody wants a switch per event type.
CHAPTER 10 — NOTIFICATIONS, EMAIL & PUSH  ·  REACHING A HUMAN
80

// Why Categories Are Derived

Event types are fine-grained and there are hundreds of them. Categories are the seven buckets a person will actually sit down and configure. The bridge between them is a lookup on the first segment of the event key, and its fallback is the interesting part.

The mapping
// Leading domain segment (before the first ".") -> category.
const DOMAIN_TO_CATEGORY = {
  auth: "security", permission: "security", role: "security", session: "security",
  approval: "approvals", workflow: "approvals", cash_request: "approvals",
  invoice: "finance", payment: "finance", journal: "finance", payroll: "finance",
  dossier: "operations", vehicle: "operations", grn: "operations", po: "operations",
  // ...
};

// "invoice.posted"  -> "invoice"  -> finance
// "vehicle.insurance.expiring" -> "vehicle" -> operations
// "widget.exploded" -> "widget"   -> NOT MAPPED -> "system"
The unmapped case falls back to system, and that choice is doing real work. The alternative — throwing on an unknown event type — means the day someone adds widget.exploded without touching this file, the notification is lost, or worse, the business transaction that triggered it rolls back. Falling back means the alert still arrives; it just lands in the general bucket until somebody classifies it. An unclassified notification is a papercut. A dropped one is a bug you find out about from a client.
Why the front end fetches this list
The preferences screen does not hardcode the seven categories. It calls GET /notifications/categories. The file comment says why: “so the UI and the enforcement logic never drift apart.”
  • Add a category to the array → it appears in the preferences UI on next load, with its label and its display order.
  • Mark one security: true → the UI can render it as locked, because it genuinely is, server-side.
  • This is the same principle as the AI action registry in Chapter 9 and the <ListPage> paved road in Chapter 7: one declaration, many consumers.
SELF-CHECK 10.1A developer adds the event subscription.renewed and does not update DOMAIN_TO_CATEGORY. What happens?
Why: Unmapped domains fall back to system. The alert still reaches the user; it is just in the general bucket until someone classifies it. Neither losing it nor failing the caller's transaction would be an acceptable price for a missing dictionary entry.

For each of these real event keys, name the category the code derives, without guessing at the meaning — trace the first segment through the map: payment.received, role.granted, milestone.completed, tax_declaration.filed, backup.failed. Which of the five cannot be silenced by the recipient, and why is that the right call?

81

// PERF S5 — The 250-Query Notification

This is the best performance war story in the repository, and it is worth studying not for the fix, which is obvious in hindsight, but for how ordinary the bug looked. Nobody wrote anything stupid. Somebody wrote a loop.

The code that was wrong
// The obvious, readable, correct-looking version:
for (const userId of recipients) {
  await notify(client, userId, { ... });
}
notify() issues roughly four to five queries: check the IN_APP preference, insert the row, check the EMAIL preference, look up the address, then send. Per recipient.
What that costs on a real event
  • invoice.posted notifies the finance group. Call it 50 users.
  • 50 × ~5 queries = ~250 sequential round-trips.
  • All of them inside an open write transaction, because the in-app row must join the caller's transaction.
  • Which means: one of the eight pooled connections pinned for the duration, and a row lock held on the invoice for the whole time.
The pathology is not the 250 queries. It is what they are holding while they run. A slow read is a slow read. A slow read inside a write transaction is a lock-duration bug wearing a performance bug's clothing, and it degrades everyone touching that row — not just the user who triggered it. This is the single most common way a healthy system falls over under load: not one catastrophic query, but a reasonable loop in a transaction that used to have three recipients and now has fifty.
SELF-CHECK 10.2Why is holding a write transaction open across 250 queries worse than running 250 queries with no transaction?
Why: The cost is contention, not raw speed. One of eight pooled connections is unavailable to everybody else, and the lock on the invoice row is held for the entire fan-out — so the blast radius is every other user touching that row, not just the one who triggered it.
CHAPTER 10 — NOTIFICATIONS, EMAIL & PUSH  ·  THE 250-QUERY NOTIFICATION
82

// The Rewrite, And What It Left Alone

Four queries, any number of recipients. But the more instructive half of this change is the fix the author could see and deliberately did not make.

Four queries, any number of recipients
  • 1All preferences, everyone, both channels — one statement. repo.preferencesFor(client, ids, ["IN_APP","EMAIL"], cat)
  • 2One multi-row INSERT for every in-app row. repo.insertForUsers(...)
  • 3All addresses — one lookup. repo.activeEmailsFor(client, emailUsers)
  • 4Then the sends, which are external I/O, not database work.
Absence of a preference row is read as IN_APP enabled, EMAIL disabled — deliberately identical to the per-user defaults the old path passed to isChannelEnabled. A bulk rewrite that quietly changed a default would be a behaviour change smuggled inside a performance fix.
The part the author refused to fix
Read this comment from the source and note what it declines to do:
// The sends stay inside the caller's transaction rather than being deferred.
// That is a deliberate limit on the scope of this change: moving them out
// means deciding what happens when the transaction rolls back after an email
// has gone, which is a correctness question, not a performance one. The queue
// already exists (BullMQ) and is the right home for them; this change removes
// the ~246 unnecessary DATABASE round-trips without touching that question.
This is senior behaviour, written down. The author could see a bigger, better fix — push the sends onto the queue from Chapter 8 — and deliberately did not take it, because it opens a correctness question (what does a sent email mean after a rollback?) that has nothing to do with the performance problem being solved. A PR that fixes one thing completely is reviewable. A PR that fixes one thing and half of another is not. Name the adjacent problem in a comment, leave it, and let it be its own decision.
SELF-CHECK 10.3The rewrite leaves the email sends inside the caller's transaction. Why is that the right call for this PR?
Why: The queue already exists and is the right eventual home. But deferring the send means deciding what happens when the transaction rolls back after the email has left, which is a correctness question, not a performance one. The PR removes 246 unnecessary round-trips and names the adjacent problem rather than half-solving it.

// Email: Two Configurations, Deliberately

SMTP is where most onboarding stalls, because there are two entirely different email systems in this product and the words for them overlap. Get the distinction straight now and the configuration is twenty minutes; get it wrong and you will debug the wrong one for a day.

The two, side by side
System emailTenant mailboxes
Whose identityThe deployment's (no-reply@…)A real human's or team's mailbox
What it sendsPassword resets, notification fan-out, alertsActual correspondence, threads, replies
Configured inPlatform Console, deploy-wideMail UI, per connection (email_connection)
ProtocolsSMTP out onlyIMAP + SMTP, or Microsoft/Google OAuth
Env keysSMTP_HOST/PORT/USER/PASSNone — stored per tenant, encrypted
These are independent. A deployment can send every password reset perfectly while no tenant has connected a single mailbox, and a tenant can be running their whole sales inbox through the Mail module while the system-email fallback is unconfigured. When someone says “email is broken”, your first question is which of the two.
The env block
# ---- Email / SMTP ---- (see doc/EMAIL_TWO_CONFIGS.md)
SMTP_HOST=__host__
SMTP_PORT=587                    # 587 STARTTLS or 465 SSL
SMTP_USER=__user__
SMTP_PASS=__rotate_me__
MAIL_FALLBACK_DOMAIN=praxisls.com
MAIL_DEFAULT_FROM=no-reply@praxisls.com
MAIL_SUPPORT_FROM=support@praxisls.com
MAIL_FALLBACK_FROM_NAME=Praxis
Every one of these has a .default() in src/config/env.js, so a deployment with no SMTP at all boots. Email degrades; the process does not die. That is the same degradation rule you met with AI keys in Chapter 9.
Precedence: platform store first, env second
STEP 1
platform_setting
mail.fallback — set and live-tested in the Platform Console. SMTP password stored encrypted.
STEP 2
env fallback
SMTP_* from the environment, for deployments configured before the console existed.
STEP 3
degrade
Neither present → sends no-op with a reason. Nothing throws.
Note which way round that is. The runtime-editable store wins over the environment, so rotating a password is a console action, not a redeploy — the same principle that makes client go-live in Chapter 13 a sequence of clicks rather than a release.
CHAPTER 10 — NOTIFICATIONS, EMAIL & PUSH  ·  EMAIL: TWO CONFIGURATIONS
84

// A Test Button That Actually Tests

“Save” is not a test. The Platform Console has a Test button beside every integration, and the SMTP one opens a real connection. Read what it does and, more importantly, what it refuses to conclude.

async function smtp(cfg) {
  if (!cfg.smtp_host) throw new Error("no SMTP host configured");
  const port = Number(cfg.smtp_port || 587);
  const nodemailer = require("nodemailer");
  const transport = nodemailer.createTransport({
    host: cfg.smtp_host,
    port,
    secure: cfg.smtp_secure === true || port === 465,
    auth: cfg.smtp_user && cfg.smtp_pass
      ? { user: cfg.smtp_user, pass: cfg.smtp_pass }
      : undefined,     // some relays authenticate by IP allowlist
  });
  await transport.verify();   // opens, EHLO/AUTH, sends nothing
  return { smtp_host: cfg.smtp_host, smtp_port: port, smtp_user: cfg.smtp_user || null };
}
Four decisions in fifteen lines
  • asecure is derived, not just declared. port === 465 implies SSL, because the single most common misconfiguration is 465 with secure:false, which hangs rather than errors.
  • bAuth is optional. Passing undefined rather than empty credentials supports relays that authenticate by IP allowlist — common for on-premise clients.
  • cverify() sends nothing. It proves connect + EHLO + AUTH. A test button that emitted real mail on every click would be a spam cannon wired to a UI control.
  • dIt returns what it proved — host, port, user — and no more. It does not report “email works”, because it has not shown that.
Point (d) is the honesty rule, and it recurs everywhere in this codebase. verify() proves the relay will accept a connection from you. It does not prove that mail you send will arrive, or survive SPF/DKIM, or stay out of spam. So the separate real-send probe returns a message with a deliberately humble note: “test email sent — check it arrives, and check the spam folder.” Compare the health endpoint in Chapter 11 that returned {ok:true} unconditionally. A check that cannot fail is not a check, and a check that overstates what it proved is worse than none, because it stops people from looking.
Failures are classified, not dumped
When verify() throws, the error is passed through mapSmtpError(), which turns raw SMTP codes into an actionable verdict — 535 is a credentials problem, 550 is a sender-verification problem — so the Platform Console can render the same fix guide the tenant console does. The user is not shown a stack trace and asked to guess.
SELF-CHECK 10.4The SMTP Test button returns success. What have you actually proven?
Why: verify() does connect, EHLO and AUTH, then stops. Deliverability — SPF, DKIM, reputation, spam placement — is untested by it, which is exactly why the real-send probe tells you to go and look in the spam folder.
CHAPTER 10 — NOTIFICATIONS, EMAIL & PUSH  ·  TESTING SMTP HONESTLY
85

// Web Push and VAPID, From Zero

Push notifications are the one part of this stack that beginners consistently believe is magic. It is not. It is four parties, one keypair, and a browser that will refuse to co-operate unless you get the order right.

The four parties
Your server
THE SENDER
  • Holds the VAPID private key
  • Signs each push request
  • Knows which user owns which device
The push service
GOOGLE / MOZILLA / APPLE
  • Run by the browser vendor, not you
  • Verifies your signature
  • Holds the message until the device is online
The browser
THE SUBSCRIBER
  • Grants or denies permission
  • Produces the subscription: endpoint + two keys
  • Wakes the service worker on delivery
The service worker
THE DISPLAYER
  • Runs with no tab open
  • Handles the push event
  • Calls showNotification()
What VAPID actually is
Voluntary Application Server Identification. It is a P-256 elliptic-curve keypair that identifies your server to the push service. That is its whole job — and note what it is not.
  • It is not encryption of the message body. That is a separate pair of keys (p256dh and auth) generated by the browser and handed to you in the subscription.
  • It is not per-user. One keypair per deployment, shared by every tenant and every device.
  • It is not a secret you buy or register. You generate it yourself, in one call, and the push service trusts it on first use.
The consequence of “one keypair per deployment” is the one that bites. Every existing subscription is bound to the public key it was created with. Rotate the VAPID keypair and every device on the deployment silently stops receiving push — no error, no bounce; the push service simply rejects the signature. There is no migration path: users must re-subscribe. Treat the keypair as permanent infrastructure, generate it once at go-live, and back up the private half with the same seriousness as a database credential.
Generating it
async function generateVapid({ subject, actor = null } = {}) {
  const webpush = require("web-push");
  const keys = webpush.generateVAPIDKeys();
  const subj = subject || "mailto:admin@praxisls.com";
  await put({
    section: "push", key: "vapid",
    value:  { public_key: keys.publicKey, subject: subj },  // readable
    secret: keys.privateKey,                                // AES-256-GCM at rest
    actor,
  });
  return { public_key: keys.publicKey, subject: subj };     // public half only
}
The split is the lesson: public key and subject go in value because the browser needs the first and the push service needs the second; the private key goes in secret, encrypted at rest with the same key as tenant secrets, and is never returned over HTTP — reads yield presence and last-4 only. The subject is a mailto: the push service can use to contact you if your traffic misbehaves.
CHAPTER 10 — NOTIFICATIONS, EMAIL & PUSH  ·  WEB PUSH: WHAT VAPID IS
86

// The Whole Push Path

Six hops, each in a file you can open. This is the flow to draw on a whiteboard when someone says push is broken, because the fault is always at one specific hop and the symptoms differ.

STEP 1
Opt in
push-opt-in.tsx — GET /notifications/push/public-key, then Notification.requestPermission().
STEP 2
Subscribe
reg.pushManager.subscribe({ userVisibleOnly: true, applicationServerKey }) returns endpoint + p256dh + auth.
STEP 3
Register
POST /notifications/push/subscribe writes the tenant push_subscription row.
STEP 4
Trigger
Something happens. notify() writes the in-app row and calls deliverPush().
STEP 5
Send
push.service.sendToUser() reads the subscriptions and posts via web-push.
STEP 6
Display
push-handler.js, imported into the Workbox SW, shows the notification and handles the tap.
Hop 1, and the base64url conversion nobody expects
function urlBase64ToUint8Array(base64String: string) {
  const padding = "=".repeat((4 - (base64String.length % 4)) % 4);
  const base64  = (base64String + padding).replace(/-/g, "+").replace(/_/g, "/");
  const raw = atob(base64);
  const out = new Uint8Array(new ArrayBuffer(raw.length));
  for (let i = 0; i < raw.length; i++) out[i] = raw.charCodeAt(i);
  return out;
}
The key is transmitted as base64url (web-safe: - and _, no padding). PushManager.subscribe demands a Uint8Array. Every web-push tutorial contains this exact function because there is no built-in for it, and skipping it produces an InvalidCharacterError that reads like a bug in your key rather than in your encoding.
Three states, not two
Read the opt-in component's state and notice it distinguishes cases most implementations collapse:
StateMeaningWhat the user is shown
!supportedNo service worker or PushManager — e.g. an old browserThe control is not offered at all
unavailableDeployment has no VAPID keypair“Not available” — not the user's fault, and not fixable by them
deniedThe user blocked notifications in the browser“Blocked in your browser settings” — a pointer to where to undo it
Collapsing these three into one “push unavailable” message is the tempting shortcut, and it produces the worst support tickets in the product. A user who blocked notifications six months ago and forgot needs to be told to check browser settings; a user on a deployment with no keypair will search their browser settings forever and find nothing wrong. The error message must name the party who can actually fix it.
SELF-CHECK 10.5A user reports push is not working. The Test button in the Platform Console says the VAPID keypair is valid. What has the probe actually established?
Why: The probe's own comment is explicit: VAPID keys cannot be exercised without a live browser subscription, so it validates format only — base64url, 87-char public, 43-char private. Same honesty rule as the SMTP probe: report what you proved, not what you hope.
CHAPTER 10 — NOTIFICATIONS, EMAIL & PUSH  ·  PUSH, END TO END
87

// How Push Fails Safely

The notification path runs inside business transactions. An unconfigured integration must therefore be incapable of failing an invoice. Two mechanisms make that true, and one of them is a bug fix worth memorising.

Every exit returns, none throws
const webpush = await configuredClient();
if (!webpush || !q) return { sent: 0, reason: "push not configured" };
let subs;
try {
  const res = await q(`SELECT endpoint, p256dh, auth FROM push_subscription WHERE user_id = $1`, [user_id]);
  subs = res.rows;
} catch {
  return { sent: 0, reason: "no push_subscription table" };   // not provisioned yet
}
{ sent: 0, reason } is a result, not an exception. The caller learns what happened and carries on. Contrast the silent-catch taxonomy from Chapter 8: this is not swallowing an error, it is returning a described outcome — the reason string is the difference between the two.
Pruning gone devices
catch (err) {
  if (err.statusCode === 404 || err.statusCode === 410) {
    await q(`DELETE FROM push_subscription WHERE endpoint = $1`, [s.endpoint]).catch(() => {});
  } else {
    logger.warn({ err }, "[push] send failed");
  }
}
404 and 410 from a push service mean the subscription is permanently gone — app uninstalled, browser data cleared, device retired. Delete it. Without this the table grows forever and every notification pays to attempt sends that can never succeed. Any other status is transient and is logged, not deleted: a network blip must not cost a user their subscription.
NEW-04, again — the require that could not fail
You met this bug in Chapter 8 and here it is in a second file. push.service.js imported config/database, whose pool is never initialised, so query resolved to a function that threw when called. There was a try/catch around it — but it guarded the require, which never failed. The failure was one level deeper, at use. Pointing the import at the pool the process actually creates is what made the fallback real.
The transferable lesson: a try/catch around an import protects you from the module being missing, not from the module being wrong. When you wrap something defensively, say out loud which failure you are catching. If the answer is vague, the guard is probably in the wrong place.
DI-4.2 — deleting a branch that never ran
sendToUser once fell back to reading shared.push_subscription via the platform pool. There is no shared schema in this system — only live, sandbox and platform — so that branch could only ever return “no push_subscription table”. Its sole caller had zero importers. Both are gone. Dead code that looks like a safety net is worse than no safety net, because the next reader budgets for a fallback that does not exist.

Your onboarding_task module gets notifications. When a task is assigned, the owner hears about it in-app, by email if they opted in, and on their phone if they subscribed a device. You will configure SMTP, generate a VAPID keypair, and prove each hop.

Part A — Emit a notification

  • Do not invent an event key prefix. Use one whose first segment already maps in DOMAIN_TO_CATEGORY, or add yours to the map in the same PR and say why in the commit.
  • Confirm the in-app row appears. This is the source of truth — if it is missing, nothing else matters.
  • Now assign a task to five users at once using notifyMany(). Count the queries in the log. Confirm it is four, not twenty-five.
Part B — Email
  • Configure mail.fallback in the Platform Console, or set SMTP_* in .env. Use a throwaway relay — never a client's production mailbox.
