  • Trigger the notification. Confirm arrival. Check the spam folder and record which folder it landed in.
  • Now break it deliberately: set SMTP_PORT=465 while leaving smtp_secure false. Observe the failure mode, then fix it.
Part C — Push
  • Generate a VAPID keypair from the Platform Console. Confirm the private key is not returned in the response body — look at the raw network response, not the UI.
  • Open the client over https:// or http://localhost. Push will not work on any other origin; this is a browser rule, not a bug in the app.
  • Subscribe in Settings. Inspect the push_subscription row and identify which of the three stored values came from the browser rather than your server.
  • Trigger the notification with the tab closed. This is the whole point of push — if it only works with the tab open, your service worker is not handling the event.
  • Tap it. Confirm notificationclick focuses the existing tab rather than opening a second one.
  • Now unsubscribe in browser settings without telling the server, and trigger again. Find the pruning branch in the log and confirm the row was deleted.

89
11
CI, Deploy & Rollback
WEEK 4 · TEACH + DRILL · ~6 HOURS · THE DEVOPS HALF

You can build the thing. This week is about getting it in front of clients and getting it back out again when it is wrong. Almost every lesson here was written down after something went badly, which is why the comments in these two shell scripts read like an incident report. They are.

The zero-downtime sequence
scripts/deploy.sh lists its own eight steps in the header, and it says plainly: “Order matters for the zero-downtime window.”
  • 1Record what is currently running, so it can be rolled back to.
  • 2Back up the database — before migrations, which have no down path.
  • 3Build new images, tagged with the commit.
  • 4Run migrations — additive by convention, so old code keeps working mid-deploy.
  • 5Restart the STANDBY api first, and wait until READY.
  • 6Restart the PRIMARY api — nginx fails over to the standby (a backup upstream) for the few seconds it is down, then traffic returns.
  • 7Restart the worker — queue downtime is invisible to users.
  • 8Verify READINESS, not just liveness.
Step 4 is the load-bearing convention. “Additive by convention” is what makes steps 5 and 6 possible at all: for a few seconds, old code and new schema are running against each other. If your migration drops a column, that window is an outage. Every migration you write is implicitly a promise about the deploy window — and you now know why the destructive-migration gate exists.
Step 8, and the endpoint that could not fail
HEALTH_URL="${HEALTH_URL:-http://localhost:3000/api/health/ready}"
  • /api/health is liveness — the process is up. No dependencies touched.
  • /api/health/ready is readiness — it probes Postgres, Redis and module loading, and returns 503 when any fails.
  • The deploy gate uses readiness. That is the whole point of having two.
CHAPTER 11 — CI, DEPLOY & ROLLBACK  ·  THE DEVOPS HALF
90

// What This Script Used To Do

The header lists four past behaviours and why each was a problem. Read all four; they are four different species of operational mistake, and you will meet every one of them somewhere in your career.

1. docker image prune -f on every deploy
“Ran on every deploy and deleted the previous image. The only artifact you could have rolled back to was destroyed by the very thing that might need rolling back. There was no rollback path at all — not a slow one, none.”
A tidy-up step, added for good reasons about disk space, quietly removed the organisation's ability to recover. Housekeeping that deletes your last known-good state is not housekeeping. The fix: KEEP_IMAGES=5 — “enough to step back more than once during a bad afternoon; few enough not to fill the disk.”
2. No backup before migrations
  • “Migrations ran against production with no dump taken first, and there is not one down-migration in the repo (DATA 3.5). A bad migration was unrecoverable.”
  • Now: BACKUP_DIR=./backups, BACKUP_KEEP=14, taken at step 2 — before anything touches the schema.
3. The health check that could not fail
“curl /api/health was the final gate. That endpoint returned {ok:true} unconditionally and never touched the database, so a container that could not reach Postgres passed the gate and the deploy printed ‘deploy ✓’.”
A gate that cannot fail is not a gate; it is a ritual. This is the operational twin of “a warning is not a gate” from Chapter 6, and of the coverage threshold that would have been satisfied by importing files. Whenever you add a check, the very next thing to do is break the system on purpose and confirm the check goes red. If you have never seen it fail, you do not know that it can.
4. Untagged images
  • “Everything was latest; nothing identified which commit was running.”
  • During an incident the first question is always what is actually deployed right now? With latest, there is no answer — only inference.
  • Now every image is tagged with its commit, and .deploy-state/ records the history.
Deploys are announced and attributed
Audit OBS-I5: “Deploys were unattributed and unannounced: nothing recorded who deployed what.” The script now announces them. In an incident, “what changed and who changed it” is the fastest route to a cause, and it is nearly free to record at deploy time and nearly impossible to reconstruct afterwards.
SELF-CHECK 11.1Which of these four failures would have been caught by a code review of deploy.sh?
Why: This is the same shape as NEW-04's wrong import: the bug lives in a relationship between artefacts, not inside one of them. curl /api/health is a perfectly sensible line — it is wrong only because of what that endpoint returned. Reviewing a file is not the same as reviewing a system.
CHAPTER 11 — CI, DEPLOY & ROLLBACK  ·  FOUR THINGS THAT WENT WRONG
91

// rollback.sh — Read It Before You Need It

The script says so itself, twice: “Read that file before you need it, not while you need it”, and “the worst time to learn what a rollback does to your database is halfway through one.”

bash scripts/rollback.sh              # back to the previous build
bash scripts/rollback.sh <commit-sha> # back to a specific one
bash scripts/rollback.sh --list       # what can I roll back to?
The warning at the top of the file
⚠ THE DATABASE IS THE HARD PART ⚠

“This script rolls back CODE. It does not, and cannot safely, roll back the SCHEMA, because there is not one down-migration in this repository (audit DATA 3.5 — ‘no migration is reversible’, still open).”
So when is a rollback safe?
SituationSafe?Why
The deploy's migrations were additive — new tables, new nullable columns, new indexesYes“The old code simply ignores them. This is the normal case and the convention the repo already follows.”
The deploy dropped or renamed anythingNo“Old code will query a column that no longer exists.”
The deploy backfilled destructivelyNoThe data the old code expects is gone.
And if it is not safe
“The database must be restored from the pre-deploy dump — which deploy.sh now always takes — and that means accepting the loss of every write since the deploy. That is a decision for a human, so this script will not make it.”
That last sentence is a design principle for every operational tool you will ever build. The script automates everything that has a correct answer, and stops dead at the point where the answer is a business trade-off — how many hours of client data are we willing to lose? A tool that made that call automatically would be faster and catastrophically wrong. Automate the mechanism; escalate the judgement.
The honest open finding
  • “still open” is written directly into the script's header.
  • DATA 3.5 has not been fixed. The team knows, the constraint is documented, and the tooling is built to be safe given it.
  • This is how mature teams carry debt: named, visible at the point of risk, with the mitigation attached — not hidden in a backlog nobody opens during an incident.
SELF-CHECK 11.2A deploy at 14:00 added a nullable column and shipped a bug. It is 14:20. What do you do?
Why: This is the normal case the convention exists to enable, and it is why “additive by convention” matters so much. Option 1 needlessly discards twenty minutes of client writes. Option 4 turns a safe code rollback into an unsafe schema change under pressure — leave the column; it is harmless.

92

// npm run ci — All Of It

scripts/ci-local.js is the authoritative list, and the same list runs locally and in CI. That is not a coincidence — it is the point.

Backend — 19 gates
GroupGates
Style & typesLint (--max-warnings 136) · Font gate
CorrectnessTest (jest) · jest.mock hoisting · No new silent catches
ConfigEnv template matches the schema
MigrationsNumbering · Reversibility · Idempotency · Destructive declared · Schema drift
SQLQuery columns exist · citext[] reads are cast · No hardcoded FX literals
API surfaceAPI docs in sync · Write routes are validated · API contract · Response-contract drift
Data integrityActor FK guard
Frontend & console — 14 gates
GroupGates
StyleLint (client, --max-warnings 112) · Raw-palette gate
Design systemDesign-token contrast · Motion budget · Frontend guide is not lying
CorrectnessTest (vitest) · Build (tsc + vite) · Bundle graph
ContractsShared schema package · Shared-schema gate
ConsoleLint / Test / Build (platform-console)
Three properties worth copying
  • 1Local and CI run the same script. No “works on my machine, fails in CI” class of problem, and no separate CI config drifting from reality.
  • 2Ratchets, not walls. 136 warnings, 112 warnings, 13% functions, a silent-catch baseline. Every one grandfathers the past and blocks regression. None of them could have been introduced as an absolute rule — the work to reach zero has never been funded, and a gate nobody can pass gets deleted.
  • 3Gates encode incidents. Almost every entry above traces to a specific defect. That is what makes the list defensible: nobody is guessing at good practice.
npm run ci          # everything (what CI runs)
npm run ci:fast     # the quick subset, for a tight loop
npm run ci:backend  # backend only
npm run ci:frontend # frontend only
Use ci:fast while you work and ci before you push. A verification loop you skip because it is slow provides zero assurance. The split exists so the honest thing is also the convenient thing — the same philosophy as the front-end paved road, applied to your own workflow.
CHAPTER 11 — CI, DEPLOY & ROLLBACK  ·  THE 33 GATES
93

// When It Breaks In Production

doc/INCIDENT_RUNBOOK.md defines four severities. Knowing which one you are in determines everything that follows — who you wake, how fast you act, and how much process you skip.

SevMeaningResponse
SEV-1Total outage, data loss, or a security breachImmediate, all hands, client comms within the hour
SEV-2A major function broken for many users; no workaroundSame day, named owner, client informed
SEV-3Degraded or broken for some; a workaround existsNext business day, tracked
SEV-4Cosmetic or minor; no functional impactNormal backlog
The first five minutes
  • 1What changed? Check the deploy announcements and .deploy-state/. Most incidents are the last deploy.
  • 2Readiness, not liveness. curl /api/health/ready. Which dependency is red?
  • 3Scope it. One tenant or all of them? A tenant-specific fault is a data or config problem; a global one is code or infrastructure.
  • 4Decide: roll back or fix forward. Additive migrations ⇒ rollback is cheap and safe. Otherwise it is a human decision about data loss.
  • 5Communicate before you are certain. “We are investigating, next update in 30 minutes” buys more goodwill than an hour of silence followed by a perfect diagnosis.
Operational commands
npm run ops:status         # queues, workers, connections
npm run ops:uptime         # the probe's view
npm run ops:alert-test     # prove the alert path works BEFORE you need it
npm run ops:sweep          # scheduled maintenance sweep
npm run db:backup:status   # is the last backup real and recent?
npm run db:restore:drill   # restore into a scratch database and verify
db:restore:drill is the most underrated command in the repository. A backup you have never restored is a hypothesis. This script tests it — and the reason the repo has it as a first-class npm script, rather than a paragraph in a runbook, is that anything requiring a human to remember to do it quarterly does not get done. The same logic as ops:alert-test: verify the recovery path on a calm day.
Writing the post-incident note
  • Timeline with real timestamps — detection, diagnosis, mitigation, resolution.
  • Client impact in the client's terms: which tenants, which function, how long.
  • Root cause, following it past the first plausible answer.
  • What made it hard to find — often the most valuable section, and the one that produces the next gate.
  • Actions, each with an owner and a date. “Be more careful” is not an action.
Notice that this repo's comments are post-incident notes. The trust proxy comment, the CORS story, NEW-04, SEC H1, F5 — each is a timeline, a root cause, and a fix, written where the next engineer will actually encounter it. That is the house style, and you are now expected to write in it.

L11
Lab — Deploy, Break, Roll Back
WEEK 4 · HANDS ON · ~2.5 HOURS · SANDBOX ONLY

Rehearse the emergency while nothing is on fire. Everything here runs against a sandbox environment — see doc/SANDBOX_TESTING.md. Confirm with your onboarding lead which environment you are pointed at before you run anything.

10.1Read first
  • Read scripts/deploy.sh end to end. All of it.
  • Read scripts/rollback.sh end to end. All of it.
  • Read doc/DEPLOYMENT.md and doc/BRANCH_PROTECTION.md.
  • Write down the one step you are least sure about, and ask about it.
10.2Deploy
  • Deploy your module to sandbox with bash scripts/deploy.sh.
  • Watch each of the eight steps. Note the wall-clock time of each.
  • Confirm the image is tagged with your commit, and that a backup was written.
  • Confirm the readiness check passed and that you know what it actually probed.
10.3Break it deliberately
  • Stop Postgres. Hit /api/health — what does liveness say?
  • Hit /api/health/ready — what does readiness say?
  • This is the OBS-A2 finding, reproduced by your own hands. Record both responses.
  • Restart Postgres and confirm readiness recovers by itself.
10.4Roll back
  • bash scripts/rollback.sh --list — what can you go back to?
  • Roll back to the previous build.
  • Verify the old version is serving, and confirm your additive migration is still present and harmless.
  • Time the whole thing. Write the number down.
The drill report40 min

Write it as though for the team: time to deploy; time to detect (from breaking Postgres to noticing); time to roll back; exactly what liveness and readiness each returned with the database down; and one improvement you would make to either script, with your reasoning. Bring this to Gate 4.

“Time to roll back” is the number that matters most, and almost no team knows theirs. It is the difference between a five-minute blip and a forty-minute outage, and it is entirely determined by rehearsal. You now know yours.
Both scripts read in fullDeployed to sandboxReadiness failure observed first-handRollback completed and timedDrill report written

Prompting The Agents
WEEK 4 · TEACH + BUILD · ~6 HOURS · THE MULTIPLIER

Claude Code, Arena and Jules. Three products, three execution models, one underlying skill: giving an agent enough context to do the work and enough scaffolding to prove it did the work. Everything in the first ten chapters — the gates, the tests, the conventions — is what makes agents useful here. This chapter is why.

The three, honestly compared
Claude CodeArena Agent ModeJules
VendorAnthropicArena.aiGoogle Labs
ExecutionSynchronous, your terminalSession workspace on a cloned repoAsynchronous, Google Cloud VM
Where code livesYour working directoryA copy of your repo in the sessionA cloned checkout in a remote VM
OutputEdits in your tree; commits and PRs if you askCommits to a working branch, opens a PRA pull request per task
SteeringContinuousConversational, mid-sessionPlan approval up front, limited after
Config fileCLAUDE.mdAGENTS.mdAGENTS.md
Best atThe one hard thing you must think aboutRepo-scoped work reviewed as a PRA queue of small, independent changes
The split is natural, not competitive. Jules takes the queue of small, independent, low-risk changes — dependency bumps, test coverage, lint fixes. Claude Code takes the one hard thing that needs a human in the loop. Arena sits where you want repo-scoped work that arrives as a reviewable pull request. Learn all three; they touch different parts of your day.
The one skill
STEP 1
EXPLORE
make it read before it writes
STEP 2
PLAN
get the approach agreed before any code
STEP 3
CODE
small, scoped, one concern
STEP 4
VERIFY
always give it a way to check itself
Explore → Plan → Code → Verify. Anthropic's own guidance for Claude Code, and it transfers unchanged to the other two. The single most common failure is skipping straight to Code — and the second most common is skipping Verify, which is the step this codebase is unusually well equipped for.
Why praxis-ls is a good agent environment
  • 33 gates that exit non-zero. An agent can run npm run ci and know, without asking you, whether it succeeded.
  • 375 tests, including structural ones that catch the “declared, not called” mistakes agents make often.
  • 131 modules in one shape. “Follow the pattern in sales/lead” is a complete, unambiguous specification.
  • Comments that explain why. The agent reads the same rationale you do — and will not innocently undo a fix whose reason is written above it.
Turn that around and it becomes the real argument for everything in Chapters 4–10. Consistency, gates and rationale comments were always good practice for humans. They are now the difference between an agent that accelerates you and an agent that generates plausible work you have to check line by line.
CHAPTER 12 — PROMPTING THE AGENTS  ·  THREE TOOLS, ONE SKILL
96

// Specific Context Beats Polite Instructions

The published guidance is consistent across all three tools and across every practitioner report: vague prompts produce vague work, and the fix is not politeness or emphasis — it is context and a success criterion.

Before and after
VagueSpecific
“Add tests for the lead module”“Test lead.rules.js for the transition out of a terminal state. Assert the error code and status. No mocks — the file is pure.”
“Fix the failing build”“npm run ci fails at ‘Query columns exist’. Run it, read the output, fix the query. Do not change the gate.”
“Make the list screen better”“OnboardingTasksPage is missing emptyFiltered. Add it following ClientsPage. Copy must differ from empty.”
“Add a module for X”“Build operations/x following src/modules/sales/lead/ exactly: same eight files, same layering. Table already exists as migration 00314. Run npm run ci:backend until green.”
Four things every good prompt contains
  • 1The exemplar. A path to a file that already does this correctly. In this repo that is nearly always available, and it is worth more than three paragraphs of description.
  • 2The boundary. What must not change. Agents are eager; scope creep is the default failure.
  • 3The verification. The exact command that proves success. npm run ci:backend, npx jest onboarding-task, npm run check:docs.
  • 4The gotcha. Anything non-obvious it cannot infer — snake_case folders, the lint ratchet, never Promise.all over req.tenantDb.
CHAPTER 12 — PROMPTING THE AGENTS  ·  WRITING THE PROMPT
97

// Guard Clauses Worth Keeping On Hand

Four paragraphs you will paste more often than any code snippet in this workbook.

# Over-eagerness
"Don't add features, refactors, or 'improvements' beyond what I asked for.
 If you think something else needs doing, tell me — don't do it."

# Reversibility and safety
"Ask before any destructive or shared-system action. Never use --no-verify.
 Never weaken a gate to make it pass."

# Anti-test-hardcoding
"Implement the general algorithm. The tests verify the behaviour; they do not
 define it. Do not special-case inputs to make a test pass."

# Verification
"After each change, run: npm run ci:backend. Paste the output. If it fails,
 fix the cause, not the check."
“Never weaken a gate to make it pass” is the single highest-value sentence you can put in a prompt in this repository. An agent facing --max-warnings 136 with 137 warnings has two ways to make the command exit zero, and one of them takes one character. It is doing what you asked. You have to say which kind of green you want.
Give it a way to see
  • Reference files with @ so it reads rather than guesses.
  • Pipe evidence in: cat error.log | claude. Paste the failing output, not your summary of it.
  • Paste screenshots for front-end work — a visual target is a verification loop.
  • The general principle: an agent with a way to check its own work behaves completely differently from one without.
SELF-CHECK 12.1Your agent's change makes npm run ci pass by adding eslint-disable comments. What went wrong in your prompt?
Why: This is Goodhart's law with a shell exit code. You asked for “exit 0” and got it. State the intent (“fix the warnings; do not suppress them; do not raise the ratchet”) and the same model produces the right work. Nearly every disappointing agent result traces back to an unstated success criterion.
CHAPTER 12 — PROMPTING THE AGENTS  ·  GUARD CLAUSES
98

// The Config File — And How To Get It Wrong

AGENTS.md is the emerging cross-tool standard; Jules and Arena read it, and Claude Code has its own CLAUDE.md. This repository currently has neither, which makes writing one an excellent Week 4 contribution — provided you write it correctly.

The research finding you must know first: in a published evaluation, an LLM-generated AGENTS.md reduced task success in five of eight settings and added 2.45–3.92 extra steps per task. Asking an agent to write its own instructions produces a plausible, comprehensive, actively harmful document. Write it by hand.
Why bloat hurts
  • The file is loaded every session, consuming context before any work starts.
  • Anthropic's guidance is to keep CLAUDE.md under about 200 lines; the wider AGENTS.md convention lands around 150.
  • A bloated file causes rules to be ignored — including the three that actually mattered.
  • Include only what the model cannot infer: commands, non-default conventions, gotchas, environment quirks, repo etiquette.
What belongs in this repo's file
SectionContent
Commands, firstnpm run dev, ci, ci:fast, ci:backend, setup:local, db:migrate:tenants. Lead with these — they are the highest-value lines.
File-scoped checksnpx jest <file> beats a full run. Prefer checks an agent can run in seconds and repeat.
Exemplars“Backend module: src/modules/sales/lead/. List screen: ClientsPage. Migration: 12743_hr_contract_doc_number.sql.”
Do / Don'tSnake_case module folders. No SQL outside .repo.js. Never Promise.all over req.tenantDb. Never raise a ratchet.
Safety splitAllowed unprompted: read, lint, test, build. Ask first: installs, git push, deletes, migrations, anything touching a shared environment.
Escape hatch“If you are stuck or the instructions conflict with the code, stop and ask — or propose a plan. Do not guess.”
And treat it as code
  • Update it in the same PR as the convention it describes. A stale AGENTS.md is F5 all over again, aimed at a machine.
  • Never put secrets in it. It is read by remote agents on cloud VMs.
  • Nested per-directory files are supported for monorepos — client/AGENTS.md could carry the eleven frontend gates.
Notice that a good AGENTS.md is just this workbook, compressed to 150 lines for a reader with no memory. If you cannot write it after finishing this document, that is useful information about which chapter to reread. If you can, you have understood the codebase — which is exactly why it is the Week 4 task.
CHAPTER 12 — PROMPTING THE AGENTS  ·  AGENTS.md
99

// Working With Each Tool

Claude Code — synchronous, supervised
  • 1Plan mode first (Shift+Tab). Make it produce the approach before it writes anything. Argue with the plan; that conversation is cheap and the code is not.
  • 2Checkpoint with git. The reported team pattern is “save state, let it run 30 minutes, then accept or start fresh” — starting fresh is a normal outcome, not a failure.
  • 3Classify the task. Async and auto-accept for peripheral work; synchronous supervision for core business logic. In this repo, that maps cleanly: a test file, yes; action-authz.js, watch every line.
  • 4Custom slash commands for anything you do twice.
  • 5Anthropic's own honest number: one-shot works about a third of the time. Plan for iteration.
Arena Agent Mode — repo-scoped, PR-delivered
  • With a repository connected, the assistant works in a copy of your repo, commits to a working branch, and opens a pull request.
  • Review the changes in the Diff tab, then merge or pull that branch.
  • Once the pull request is merged or closed, the session can no longer push. Anything created after that stays in the session and cannot be pushed, downloaded, or carried into a new session.
  • So: push before you merge, and start a fresh session for new work. That is a real operational rule, not a detail.
  • With no repository connected, files live in the session workspace and are downloaded as a zip.
The branch-scoped session model is a feature, not a limitation. It forces the same discipline as branch protection: work arrives as a reviewable diff on a branch, and merging is a deliberate human act that closes the session. It fits this repo's BRANCH_PROTECTION.md workflow exactly.
Jules — asynchronous, plan-gated
  • 1Point it at a GitHub repository and branch, and describe one specific task.
  • 2It clones into a cloud VM, then writes a plan and waits for your approval. Read the plan properly — if you wander off, a timer may auto-approve it.
  • 3It executes in the background, runs your tests, and opens a PR. You review it like any teammate's.
  • 4Best for: test generation, bug fixes from a symptom, dependency bumps, documentation. Worst for: anything needing continuous steering.
  • 5Practitioner consensus: async agents need validation loops, tests, and issues broken into small chunks with the where and why stated. That is a description of this repository.
The common thread. All three deliver a diff you must review. None of them removes your responsibility for the code — and the review is where your Chapters 1–10 knowledge earns its keep. An agent makes a competent engineer faster; it makes an engineer who cannot review the output dangerous.
CHAPTER 12 — PROMPTING THE AGENTS  ·  THREE WORKFLOWS
100

// The Trust-Then-Verify Gap

The named anti-pattern. Agent output is fluent, well-formatted, confidently commented and frequently correct — which is exactly what makes the incorrect fraction so dangerous. Fluency is not evidence.

Where agents fail in this codebase specifically
FailureHow to catch it
Declared, not calledIt adds a middleware but does not mount it; a handler with no producer; a manifest entry with no catalogue row. Run the wiring sweep.
Plausible column namesIt writes client_type because that is the obvious name. The real column is client_type_id. npm run db:check:columns.
Mocking the interesting boundaryThe test passes and proves nothing. Read every jest.mock it added and ask what it hides.
Silent catchesDefensive try/catch everywhere, all empty. The silent-catch gate, and your own eyes.
Weakening a gateeslint-disable, a raised ratchet, a deleted assertion. Read the diff for changes to config and test files, first.
Layer violationsSQL in the service because it was two lines shorter. Read the repo/service boundary in every diff.
Fail-open defaultsA new state added to NEXT but not to TRANSITION_ACTION, with a permissive fallback invented. Check the fail-closed direction.
Read the diff in this order, always: config files → test files → migrations → source. Config and test changes are where a green build gets manufactured, and they are the smallest, easiest part of the diff to skim past. If a “fix the tests” task changed the tests rather than the code, you need to know that in the first ten seconds.
The review questions
  • Did it change any gate, threshold, baseline or lint directive? Why?
  • Does every new catch either handle, log, or carry a taxonomy marker?
  • Is every new mock justified — and what would slip past it?
  • Does the new code follow the eight-file layering, or has logic leaked?
  • Are new lookup tables and defaults fail-closed?
  • Is anything declared but not called? Run the sweep, do not eyeball it.
  • Would I have written the migration header this way? Does it say what is lost?
  • Can I explain every line to my onboarding lead? If not, it does not merge.
That last question is the standard, and it is not negotiable. You are accountable for what you merge, regardless of what wrote it. “The agent did it” has never been an acceptable answer about a line of code, and it never will be.
CHAPTER 12 — PROMPTING THE AGENTS  ·  REVIEWING AGENT WORK
101
L12
Lab — Delegate Something Real
WEEK 4 · HANDS ON · ~3 HOURS

Three tasks, deliberately chosen so one should succeed, one should need iteration, and one should expose a limit. The deliverable is not the code — it is your judgement about when to delegate.

11.1Task A — well-scoped (should succeed)
  • Ask an agent to add the db-layer tests for your repo's list filters.
  • Give it: the exemplar test file, the file under test, and npx jest onboarding-task as the verification.
  • Record the prompt verbatim.
  • Review against the seven failure modes. Note anything you had to fix.
11.2Task B — needs iteration
  • Ask it to add a ?sort= parameter to your list endpoint, matching resolveSort in the CRUD kit.
  • Do not mention the allow-list requirement. See whether it discovers it.
  • If it builds an ORDER BY from user input unguarded, that is SEC H3 recurring — record exactly how it got there.
  • Then reprompt with the constraint and compare the two attempts.
11.3Task C — should expose a limit
  • Ask it to decide whether assigning a PENDING task should auto-advance it to IN_PROGRESS, and to implement its choice.
  • This is a product decision with no right answer in the code.
  • Record what it did: did it choose confidently, hedge, or ask?
  • Write what this tells you about which decisions you may delegate.
The delegation memo45 min

Write the memo for the team: (1) the three prompts verbatim; (2) what each produced; (3) time spent prompting and reviewing versus your estimate of writing it yourself; (4) which of the seven failure modes you actually saw; (5) your rule for what you will and will not delegate in this codebase. Point (5) is the real output.

Then write the file
  • Draft AGENTS.md for this repository. By hand. Under 150 lines.
  • Commands first. Exemplar paths. Do/Don't. The safety split. The escape hatch.
  • Test it: run Task A again in a fresh session with the file present. Did it need fewer corrections?
  • Bring it to Gate 4. If it is good, it ships — and every engineer after you benefits.
This is the highest-leverage thing a new engineer can contribute in their first month. You have just read the whole codebase with fresh eyes and written down what confused you. That is precisely the perspective a good AGENTS.md requires, and precisely the perspective everyone loses after six months here.
Three tasks delegated and reviewedFailure modes recordedDelegation rule writtenAGENTS.md hand-written and tested
CHAPTER 12 — PROMPTING THE AGENTS  ·  LAB 11 — DELEGATE AND VERIFY
102
13
Shipping To A Client
WEEK 4 · TEACH + REHEARSE · ~5 HOURS

Everything until now was engineering. This chapter is the part that decides whether the engineering was worth anything: provisioning a tenant, configuring it, proving it, training the people who will use it every day, and staying close while they learn. At JBS Praxis, engineers do this. It is not someone else's job.

Why the engineer is in the room
  • You know which errors are configuration and which are defects — class G versus everything else.
  • You know what the sandbox does differently, so you can demonstrate safely without inventing a fake environment.
  • You know what the system cannot do, and saying so early is worth more than any feature.
  • And you learn what the software is actually for. Every good decision in Chapters 3–9 came from somebody understanding the business — “one is a default, two is a question” is not a programming insight.
The shape of a go-live
STEP 1
PROVISION
schema, admin, plan
STEP 2
CONFIGURE
brand, mail, AI, FX — tested at runtime
STEP 3
SEED & REHEARSE
sandbox, realistic data, the full flow
STEP 4
TRAIN
by role, on their own data
STEP 5
HYPERCARE
close support while habits form
The goal stated at the end of the official checklist is the one to internalise: “Record anything that needed a config change, not a key entry, in the tenant's handover note — the goal is that the NEXT tenant needs only keys and brand assets.” Every onboarding should make the next one shorter. If yours needed code, that is a finding, not a chore.
Provisioning
npm run db:provision -- --slug=acme --name="Acme Logistics" --plan=standard
npm run db:migrate:tenants
npm run tenant:create-admin -- --slug=acme --email=… --name="…"

# Locally, all of it in one:
npm run setup:local -- --slug=acme --name="Acme Logistics" --with-worker
Before you start, the official checklist requires: the tenant is provisioned with status = LIVE, the admin user exists and can sign in, and you hold a Settings (MOD-70) edit grant — every runtime test is capability-gated on settings.write. Keep the tenant URL to hand: https://<slug>.praxisls.com.
CHAPTER 13 — SHIPPING TO A CLIENT  ·  THE LAST MILE
103

// Eight Sections, Every One Tested At Runtime

doc/TENANT_ONBOARDING_CHECKLIST.md is the operator's checklist. Its defining property: “every step is a click or a curl in the running app — none of them require a redeploy”, and each step ends in a test, not a saved form.

1Branding (white-label)
  • Logo and login background; save and hard-refresh the login page.
  • Brand colours — confirm the login page repaints without a deploy (live CSS variables).
  • PWA identity: the install prompt must use the tenant's name and icon.
  • Verify the “Powered by JBS Praxis LLC” footer is present on login.
2Sending identity (SMTP)
  • SMTP host/port/credentials plus a verified identity for at least one purpose.
  • POST /api/platform/settings/mail.default/test → { ok: true } and a probe email must actually arrive.
  • Then send a real document: issue a test invoice, Send from the viewer, confirm an email_send_log row with status SENT.
3AI providers
  • Add the tenant's keys: vision, voice, generation, embeddings.
  • POST /api/platform/ai-vendors/<vendor>/test per vendor. “A failed key answers with the provider's error, not a timeout.”
  • AI Control: per-user and per-tenant spend caps and feature flags. Sandbox is always mock.
  • Generate a PDF. If it fails, the worker image lacks Chromium or PUPPETEER_EXECUTABLE_PATH is unset.
4FX rates
  • Enable the source and paste the key; trigger Sync now.
  • Confirm a real conversion returns the new rate.
  • Confirm fx-sync is in the worker's registered repeatables — otherwise rates only move when someone clicks.
Section 4's last item is Chapter 8 arriving in the field. A worker with no scheduler is a job nobody starts — and the client would discover it weeks later as quietly stale exchange rates on their invoices. The checklist exists because someone lived that. Every checklist item is a scar.
Why runtime tests, not saved settings
A saved SMTP password proves someone typed a password. { ok: true } plus an email in an inbox proves the system can send mail. The distinction between “configured” and “working” is where go-lives fail, and it is the same distinction as the health endpoint that returned {ok:true} unconditionally, and the coverage gate satisfied by importing files. You have now seen this idea in three completely different parts of the system.
SELF-CHECK 13.1A client's AI vendor key is wrong. What should the test endpoint return?
Why: The checklist specifies this explicitly. A timeout tells the operator nothing and sends them to check firewalls. The provider's error message — “invalid API key” — tells them exactly what to fix. This is class G from the error taxonomy: a configuration problem with a fix-it path, never an engineering page.
CHAPTER 13 — SHIPPING TO A CLIENT  ·  THE CONFIGURATION CHECKLIST
104

// Rehearse On Real-Shaped Data

doc/SANDBOX_TESTING.md: “get a tenant's sandbox schema populated with realistic Cameroon freight-forwarder data so every built screen shows something, then walk the whole app end-to-end without risking live data.”

What the seed gives you
  • 2 corporate entities, 6 clients, 5 suppliers, 8 employees, 3 treasury accounts, 5 dossiers at different stages.
  • The whole sales funnel — leads → meetings → campaigns → opportunities across every pipeline stage → proposals.
  • Commercial, finance documents, fixed assets, the full fleet, WMS, procurement (PR → PO → GRN), and HR.
  • Realistic, domain-correct data — not test1, test2, asdf. This matters enormously for training.
And what it deliberately does not
“It does not post to the general ledger.” Because it is direct SQL rather than the service layer, it does not write journal_entry / journal_line rows — “that keeps it clear of the ledger invariant triggers (balanced / gap-free entry_no / mandatory source_doc_ref)”. Finance documents are seeded in pre-posting states with entry_id = NULL.
Read the consequence, and then read how it is handled. “Trial balance, financial statements, and true receivables ageing are empty until you post real entries — and posting is exactly what you should test through the app.” The gap is not an oversight; it is deliberately left as the thing the operator must exercise. And so the dashboard is not simply blank, the seed sets cached_receivables and cached_overdue so the tiles still show numbers. A limitation, documented, mitigated, and turned into a test.
Sandbox hygiene — the three guards
In TEST modeWhat happens
Sending an emailRecorded as SUPPRESSED — it never leaves the server
Generating a PDFWatermarked TEST SANDBOX
AI generationTakes the mock path — no spend, no egress
  • Spot-check all three before you put a client in front of the sandbox. The checklist says so.
  • sandbox_wipe_days defaults to 14; confirm the daily scheduler tick appears in the worker log.
  • Remember the environment rule from Chapter 1: sandbox is active only when !tenant.is_live and the request carries X-Praxis-Env: sandbox.
A real gotcha, documented with a date
⚠ Machine/DB switch (2026-07-22). If a login user was re-created in live with a new user_id while the sandbox still holds the old row for the same email, every TEST-mode write fails with 409 Referenced record not found (FK 23503 on the actor user). The seed now tombstones the stale row's unique email/username and mirrors the new one — so the fix is simply to re-run the seed, no wipe needed.
That is what a good gotcha note looks like: the symptom the operator will actually see, the underlying cause, the date it was found, and a one-line fix. Write yours this way. You will meet it on someone else's laptop in six months.
CHAPTER 13 — SHIPPING TO A CLIENT  ·  SANDBOX & REHEARSAL
105

// The Parts Clients See That You Never Look At

Sections 6 and 7 of the checklist. These surfaces are used by people who do not work for your client — their customers, their auditors, the public — which makes them the least forgiving part of the system.

The portal
  • Invite a test client contact via Settings → Portal Access.
  • Sign in at /portal and confirm the client terminal renders.
  • Do this as the contact would, in a clean browser profile. A portal that works only in your logged-in session is not tested.
The public site
  • /public loads; the quote form posts an intake row into the sales queue.
  • /public/track answers 404 — not 401 — for an unknown reference.
  • Careers and portfolio pages render.
Why 404 and not 401 on an unknown tracking reference? Because 401 says “this exists, you just cannot see it”. On a public endpoint that is an enumeration oracle: an attacker can discover which reference numbers are real by watching the status code. 404 for both “does not exist” and “not yours” leaks nothing. This is the same care about status codes as WRONG_HOST, the CORS 403 and LOCKED 422 — chosen for what it reveals as much as what it means.
The auditor data room
  • Grant an AUDITOR portal access.
  • Raise a data-room request from the portal.
  • Attach a VERIFIED vault document as staff.
  • Confirm the auditor can download it — end to end, as both parties.
God Mode
  • CEO → God Mode → Set PIN, or wait for the weekly rotation email.
  • Confirm purge works, and that an expired PIN is refused after 7 days.
  • Test the refusal, not just the success. An expiry nobody has watched expire is an assumption.
Notice the pattern across every section of this checklist: test the thing working, then test the thing refusing. Send the email and check the suppression. Download as the auditor and confirm the expired PIN is rejected. Half of correctness is refusing correctly — and it is the half nobody demonstrates in a demo.
CHAPTER 13 — SHIPPING TO A CLIENT  ·  EXTERNAL SURFACES & GOD MODE
106

// Training People, Not Demonstrating Software

The most common failure is a beautiful two-hour walkthrough of every screen, after which nobody can do their own job. Train by role, on their data, with their hands on the keyboard.

Four rules
  • 1By role, not by module. A finance clerk does not need the fleet screens. Build a session per role around the five things that person does daily.
  • 2On their own data. Their client names, their dossier references, their currencies. Generic demo data teaches the software; their data teaches their job in the software.
  • 3They drive. If you are holding the keyboard, you are the only person learning. Talk them through it; do not do it for them.
  • 4Teach the error states. What a 422 looks like, what “already revoked” means, what to do when a PDF does not arrive. Confidence comes from having already seen the thing go wrong once, in a room with you in it.
Rule 4, made concrete
Deliberately trigger, in front of them: a validation error with a highlighted field; an action on a locked record; an idempotent no-op showing “that was already done”; and an offline save that queues and replays. Those four moments prevent more support tickets than any amount of happy-path training — because each one is otherwise interpreted as “the system is broken”.
A session plan
SessionWhoContent
Admin (2h)Tenant adminUsers, roles, permissions, branding, settings, God Mode boundaries
Operations (2h)Ops staffDossiers end to end, milestones, documents, the four error states
Commercial (90m)Sales & commercialLeads → qualification → conversion, quotations, costings
Finance (2h)FinanceInvoices, posting, receivables, FX — and what posting means, because the sandbox cannot rehearse it
Copilot (45m)EveryoneWhat it can do, that it cannot exceed your own permissions, and why writes always confirm
The copilot session is different
  • Users need to know the assistant runs as them — it cannot do what they cannot do. This is reassuring, and it is true because of Chapter 9.
  • They need to know every write asks first, and that they should read the card, not reflex-click. Say why: confirmations that appear everywhere stop being read.
  • They need to know sensitive data is redacted before it leaves, and that sandbox AI is mocked.
  • Explain the limits honestly. A user who trusts it for everything will be burned; a user who trusts it for nothing wasted your integration.
Write the one-page role card40 min

Pick one role and write the single page they keep beside their screen: their five daily tasks as numbered steps, the four error states with what to do about each, and who to contact. One page. If it needs two, you have not understood the role yet.

CHAPTER 13 — SHIPPING TO A CLIENT  ·  TRAINING THE CLIENT
107

// The First Two Weeks

Go-live is not the end of a project; it is the start of the only period in which the client decides whether they trust the system.

H1Days 1–3 — presence
  • Someone available on a channel the client actually uses, within minutes.
  • A daily check of ops:status, the error monitor, and the mail send log.
  • Log every question. Questions are the highest-quality product feedback you will ever get.
  • Fix configuration immediately; queue defects properly — and be able to tell the two apart out loud.
H2Days 4–14 — withdrawal
  • Move from “we are watching” to “raise a ticket”, deliberately and with a date.
  • A weekly review of error rates, queue depth, and slow endpoints.
  • Convert the recurring questions into training material or a UI change.
  • Confirm backups are running and run a restore drill against the new tenant.
H3The handover note
  • Everything that needed a config change rather than a key entry.
  • Anything client-specific a future engineer would be surprised by.
  • The role cards, and who was trained on what.
  • Open items, with owners and dates.
The handover note is the deliverable that makes the next go-live cheaper. The checklist's stated goal — that the next tenant needs only keys and brand assets — is only reachable if every onboarding writes down what it had to work around. An undocumented workaround is a permanent tax on everyone who comes after you.
Escalation, so nobody has to guess
ConfigurationYou fix it now. Log it in the handover note.
Training gapYou fix it now, and update the role card.
SEV-3/4 defectTicket, owner, date. Tell the client the date and then meet it.
SEV-1/2 defectIncident runbook. Tell the client before they tell you.
“Tell the client before they tell you” is the whole of client trust in six words. A team that reports its own outage is a team that is watching. A team that learns of its outage from the client is a team that is not — and no amount of technical excellence recovers that impression.
CHAPTER 13 — SHIPPING TO A CLIENT  ·  HYPERCARE & HANDOVER
108
G4
Gate 4 — Graduation
THE FINAL GATE · SIGNED OFF BY YOUR ONBOARDING LEAD

The last gate, and the only one with a single deliverable: the graduation PR. Everything you built across four weeks, merged as one reviewable change, defended in person.

The graduation PR contains
  • The migration from Lab 4B, with a full house-style header and a -- DOWN block.
  • The eight-file module from Chapter 5, mounted and working.
  • The four layers of test from Lab 6, plus your anti-drift test from Chapter 6.
  • The list screen and create dialog from Lab 7, on the paved road.
  • The background job and its scheduler from Lab 8, both halves.
  • The AI action from Lab 9, with its adversarial authz test.
  • AGENTS.md, hand-written, under 150 lines.
  • A QA note, a drill report, and a delegation memo.
And it must be
G4.1Green
  • npm run ci passes — all 33 gates.
  • No gate weakened. No raised ratchet, no eslint-disable, no deleted assertion, no --no-verify.
  • The coverage floor holds.
G4.2Defensible
  • You can explain every line, including any an agent wrote.
  • Every non-obvious decision is in a comment that says why not the obvious alternative.
  • You can name what you deliberately did not do, and why.
G4.3Demonstrated live
  • Walk the full vertical slice — screen, API, service, SQL, job, copilot.
  • Show the four error states as a user would meet them.
  • Show the ungranted user being refused on the AI action.
  • Roll back your sandbox deploy, and state your time-to-rollback.
G4.4Taught back
  • Teach one chapter's core idea to the next new engineer, for twenty minutes.
  • Answer their questions without notes.
  • Log what you could not answer — that list is your next month.
PR open and greenEvery line defensibleSlice demonstratedRollback timedTaught backLead signed off
G4.4 is not a formality. Teaching is the only reliable test of understanding, and the questions a beginner asks are the ones that find the edge of what you actually know. Every engineer who passes this gate teaches the next one — that is how this document stays alive and how the standard survives the person who wrote it.
JBS PRAXIS ENGINEERING WORKBOOK — GATE 4 — GRADUATION
109

// Twenty Things This Codebase Believes

Every one of these is a sentence you can trace to a file, and most of them to an incident. This is the page to reread when you are about to make a decision you have not made before.

On safety
  • 1Fail closed. The missing case is the safe case. Unlisted transition → approve; unmatched identifier → rejected; undeclared permission → does not run.
  • 2Visibly broken beats invisibly open. Choose the failure someone will report within the hour.
  • 3Recording is not preventing. A perfect audit trail of unauthorised actions is still unauthorised actions.
  • 4Never let a value become syntax. Parameterise; validate identifiers in one place nobody can bypass.
  • 5Reject, do not silently drop. A filter that is ignored returns more than asked for, and looks like success.
On verification
  • 6A warning is not a gate. If it must not reach production, something must exit non-zero.
  • 7A gate that cannot fail is a ritual. Break the system on purpose and watch it go red.
  • 8Every mock is an assumption you stopped checking. Never mock the boundary the bug lives at.
  • 9Measure before you set a threshold. A guessed number either blocks the first build or means nothing forever — and both end with the gate deleted.
  • 10Ratchets, not walls. Baseline the past, block the regression, pay down opportunistically.
On design
  • 11One owner of the boundary. Transactions, identifiers, mail sends, event emission — one place, so it cannot be forgotten.
  • 12Declared is not called. Six shapes of it, one test suite to hunt them.
  • 13An abstraction people escape is worse than none. Draw the boundary where screens genuinely agree.
  • 14One is a default, two is a question. LIMIT 2, not LIMIT 1.
  • 15Make the correct thing the easy thing. A generator beats a convention document, every time.
On people
  • 16Comments explain why not the obvious alternative. That is the only comment worth writing.
  • 17Write down the cost of a trade-off at the point you make it, or someone discovers it as a bug.
  • 18Automate the mechanism; escalate the judgement. Rollback scripts stop where data loss begins.
  • 19Design the fix so the transition can be incremental, and you will actually finish it.
  • 20Tell the client before they tell you.

Final Examination
THE LAST THING · 20 QUESTIONS · 80% TO PASS

One written examination, drawn at random from a bank covering all thirteen chapters. It is not a memory test: every question is about a decision this codebase made and why it made it. If you did the labs, you have already met all of it.

Unlocking the examination
Three conditions, tracked automatically as you work through the workbook. They are shown live below — the ticks appear as you satisfy them.

Not yet attempted. 80% required to pass.

Your certificate
Pass, and the workbook issues a certificate in your name carrying your score, the number of pages completed, and a reference number derived from your name and sitting. It downloads as a landscape A4 PDF.
Certificate of Completion

Issued to the name you enrolled with. Your best score is the one printed — re-sitting to improve it is study, not cheating, and a fresh set of questions is drawn each time.

An honest note about the gate, since you are an engineer and will work this out anyway. All of this runs in your browser, and the progress record is a key in localStorage. You could open DevTools and mark everything complete in about fifteen seconds. The gate is a study aid, not a security control, and pretending otherwise to this audience would be exactly the kind of dishonest check Chapter 11 spends a page criticising. The certificate is worth what the work behind it is worth. Your onboarding lead signs Gate 4, and they will know.

113
// END OF WORKBOOK

Now Go
Build Something

You arrived able to write SQL. You can now read a 1,225-file codebase, build a feature through every layer of it, test it four ways, ship it, roll it back, delegate part of it to an agent and review what comes back, and put it in front of a client who has never seen it before.

That is the whole job. Everything after this is repetition, depth, and the particular problems of whichever system you are handed next — and most JBS Praxis projects follow this format, so you have already met most of it.

Two last things. Keep writing the comments that explain why not the obvious alternative — they are how this codebase taught you, and they are how you will teach the next person. And when you find the gate whose message is unhelpful, the document that is lying, or the workaround nobody wrote down: fix it, and say so. That is what everyone before you did, and it is the only reason any of this was learnable.
